speakerposition: stagedirection
Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just voted on a motion that gags the House, invokes closure and, in my opinion, reveals the extent of this government's incompetence and total inability to manage the House's time. For several weeks, it has been resorting to unparliamentary and almost undemocratic practices.
Mr. Speaker, this vote to invoke closure of the debate on motion No. 26, that is on a government motion to extend this sitting which, as we all know, began on August 11 of last year, effectively extends this sitting until Friday September 9, 1988. This means that the House will not adjourn for the summer, in accordance with the Standing Orders. Moreover, daily sittings will be extended until 10 p.m., creating, as we know, problems with families who, in many cases, are not here in Ottawa. MPs will therefore not be able to spend time with their children.


I want the government to know that I think the motion before us is shameful and goes against parliamentary practice since it invokes closure and places the Opposition in a difficult situation.
Mr. Speaker, what the Government did today when they moved to consider the orders of the day at 11 a.m, at the beginning of the proceedings, well they could have done that last week, on Wednesday, Thursday or Friday at 10 a.m., when the Government order was called. The fact is they didn't.
Why? Because it suited their purpose to prolong the debate a little, to make Canadians think that there was some resistance on the part of the Official Opposition or the NDP. But their primary intention was to attract the media's attention. There was one editorial on the subject this morning, and I have spoken to several Conservative Members who have said to me:

"We have an editorial in The Globe and Mail. Did you read it?" I did, Sir. I read it, yes. I was not very much impressed with it because the facts of it are not very impressive. The Government has been snapping its suspenders and saying, "we have an editorial, finally," after holding the Elouse of Commons for three solid days last week, a waste of time-

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext: We were not holding it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext:
Yes, you were. Members of the Government held the House of Commons last week for three solid days. They now have an editorial in The Globe and Mail. How much begging that cost, I do not know.
I remind government Members that The Globe and Mail is the national newspaper-if they are going to hold this up as anything more than a piece of paper-that was found in contempt by the House on December 22, 1976. I wish to put the matter into context.
I wish to read the motion adopted unanimously pursuant to Standing Order 43. It was moved by Mr. MacEachen and seconded by Mr. Baker, the former Member for Grenville- Carleton, who is now deceased, that a statement contained in an editorial in The Globe and Mail was a gross libel of Mr. Speaker, and that the publication of the article was a gross breach of the privileges of this House.
That was the only time in the history of Parliament that I know of, in my 15 years here, that a newspaper was found to be guilty of contempt of the House of Commons. Members opposite are waving this morning's editorial saying, "Look at that. We have a great newspaper article saying that we were right last week". They were not right last week, and they know it. They did it intentionally. They left the House hanging because they refused to use the rules to assist their purpose, which is to order Government Business.
Extension of Sittings

Mr. Speaker, I said it last week, I said it last Wednesday and again last Thursday in the House, after each vote in which only the Liberal Party Whip participated, the government could have used a provision in the Standing Orders which would have allowed it, during Routine Proceedings, to call the orders of the day. Why didn't they do this either on Wednesday, Thursday or Friday?

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext: Because they didn't want to!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext:
I don't know, but they wanted to shift the blame for the delay to the Opposition. Well, Mr. Speaker, they showed poor judgment, as usual, and in my opinion, they acted irresponsibly and displayed their incompetence and inability to manage the time of this House.
It's so obvious, Mr. Speaker, that this Government is awkward .. .

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext: Clumsy!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext: ... clumsy-I thank the Hon. Member for Hamilton-East (Ms. Copps)-when it comes to managing its affairs. They looked like a bunch of fools about a month ago, Mr. Speaker ...

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext: They are!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext:
.. . when they sent a letter to the Official Opposition House Leader dated May 30. That was barely a month ago-no, I'm sorry, it was in fact only a few weeks ago. In this letter dated May 30, they indicated their desire to see the three parties in the House reach an agreement to pass 23 bills at different stages, and said that five Bills on the Order Paper could perhaps be adopted .. .

I should read this because it is in English. There were 11 Bills not yet introduced, something which was contained in the letter of May 30 signed by the Minister of State for the Treasury Board (Mr. Lewis). There was everything from the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program, to child care, to film and video, disabled persons, transportation, and income tax reform. We finally got the Bill on income tax reform. It was in the form of a Ways and Means motion. It is a huge package.
Members of the Government want this, plus those 11 pieces of legislation not yet introduced, plus a major debate on abortion, a major debate on Meech Lake, and a major debate on free trade. They want that, all in the space of less than 20 days. How foolish can they take us to be? How do they play the Canadian public to eat this up and to believe this nonsense?
Just to give the House an idea of the complexity of the tax reform Bill, I looked into it.


Extension of Sittings

I looked into several Standing Orders to see if it was possible, in the space of a few days, to go through the entire Bill. Mr. Speaker, I will give the benefit of the doubt to the experts in this field, namely the Joint Committee on Taxation of the Canadian Bar Association-these are no fools-and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, who also are very knowledgeable in this area. Here is what they had to say about this Bill in a brief submitted in May 1988, not two years, but rather barely one month ago, and 1 quote: "The provisions of the draft Bill pertaining to automobile costs and related benefits are extremely complex. A total of 30 different amendments had to be made to the Act and the relevant regulations to translate into legal terms the proposed measures contained in the White Paper as amended in December 1987.
These provisions are full of technical errors, which proves that even those who wrote them have a great deal of trouble understanding the regulations". These are not my words, but rather those of Canada's accountants and lawyers who examined the bill, the voluminous, 500-page Bill that the government wanted to pass in just a few days. That makes no sense at all, Mr. Speaker. The purpose of tax reform as to simplify matters and make them less complex. That has not happened, Mr. Speaker. They have complicated matters, even for the Canadian Bar Association and for our country's accountants. And here in the House of Commons, we would like to settle this matter quickly, in a matter of days! That is our idea of democracy.
We love to have things done our way. We said: "Just a minute. The people of Canada want to hear the debate. They want to have this thing looked at sincerely and with the intent of possibly strengthening it and avoiding some of the mistakes we know the Government is prone to making".
The Government called us back on August 11, last year, for an emergency session. A boatload of Sikhs landed in Nova Scotia and an emergency was declared. Those two Bills are still before the House.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext:
They don't like to hear the truth, Mr. Speaker. Motion No. 26, which would suspend the Standing Orders and allow the government Order, effectively cancels the summer adjournment. We the Members of the Opposition are prepared to work diligently. If the Government wishes to call bills and to debate them seriously, then we are prepared to work with them, to deal with the legislation on the table. We are quite prepared for daily Question Period and quite willing to let journalists report what they see and rap the government on the knuckles when it deserves it. And it very often deserves it.

We do not mind that, Mr. Speaker. It would cost us a fortune to have that media coverage every day. "Go ahead", I say to the Government, "sit all summer; sit July and August". We will have, I think, the benefit of having Members over there down in the polls in August while we will be going up. It is an old truism that when the House sits, Governments go down in the polls and the Opposition goes up. So I say: "Go ahead. Do you think we care?" We would just as soon be here, and we will debate this.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext: the second session and three during the first session, for a total of eight. In all, 203 pieces of legislation have been passed by the House. That's not so bad. That's about average, when we look at past governments.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext:
The numbers for the past four years are around 200, 210, 215. No more, but no less. I hear some nos. You weren't here at the time, so how could you know! I say to you that this is about average. We might not have worked miracles, or invented a better mousetrap, but we haven't done too badly. The reason is because the Opposition has been willing to work with the Government. When the Government is serious, we are more than willing to go along with it. However, when the Government behaves irresponsibly, like some of the hon. Members before me, we can only do so much. When the Government proposes, we dispose. However, when the Government doesn't propose anything, how can we do anything?
There is a series of Bills now before us, Mr. Speaker. A while ago, I reminded the House of the 39 or so Bills that the Government wanted to take up, in addition to two or three important debates. It's sad to say, Mr. Speaker, but the Government is being irresponsible if it thinks that the House of Commons should deal with 40 Bills in less than one month when, as I just explained, it has dealt with nearly 200 over a period of four years. It means that the Government wants us to accomplish in one month's time what normally takes us about one year to do! It's trying to push and hurry the Opposition, don't you see! It's trying to influence public opinion through an editorial in the Globe and Mail and trying to fend off the Opposition. Well, Mr. Speaker, it's going to take more than an article in the Globe and Mail to fend us off when we know that the government could, if it had had any guts and backbone, have tabled these Bills in an orderly fashion in the House.
They are asking us to spend five days on the Mulroney-Reagan Agreement, that is the free trade agreement with the United States. This agreement has the potential of altering Canada's business and economic future. They want us to spend only a few days on tax reform. I Assume that the Government was serious when it stated in its letter of May 30 that it wanted to spend a few days on this subject. The fiscal and economic future of our country is at stake here! They asked us to deal with Meech Lake quickly and we did. The Government got its way, and the first vote has taken place and the other ones will be taken on Wednesday at 3 p.m. The official languages Bill has been before the House since June 25. It was called last February 8 or 9. It was referred to a committee on March 9. The committee met in an emergency session on March 17. It's now June 20, Mr. Speaker, and the Bill has been before the committee for three months. The Government is not even scheduling meetings of the committee. Why is this? Because the Conservative caucus disagrees on the scope of the Official Languages Act. They are putting their personal interests
Extension of Sittings
before those of Canadians. The passage of Bill C-72 is being delayed, through no fault of the Opposition. We have told them to pass the bill as is. But they answer that they have some issues to resolve between themselves. That particular piece of legislation will also affect our country's future.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext: Arguments between Neanderthals.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext:
Indeed. And here we are being asked to move quickly on 40 Bills, including those that I just mentioned, and some others as well. It's ridiculous! And they know it is. Can the Government be so incompetent as to suggest that the House do the impossible? If this it true, then it's sad for the country.
Mr. Speaker, the government was very pleased with its tax reform proposals.
You remember the government supported tax reform. We have seen the tax reform bill and it will take more than three days to wade through it and pass it. The government has to be reasonable. If it is prepared to refer it to a committee after a serious debate in the Commons, we have no objections to that.
The Government also claimed to support parliamentary reform. A committee chaired by Mr. McGrath considered reform for two or three years and did a good job of it. The Government couldn't say enough about how a reformed House would be a great improvement and how backbenchers on both sides would finally have more power to change things. But, we know that nothing has changed. They have even trampled the Standing Orders with motion no. 26. And why have they done this? To impose their will and their ideas on the House.
It's a shame, Mr. Speaker, but democracy will only be better served when this Government is defeated and replaced by another.
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with incompetent people. Bourinot speaks of "evidence of the lack of foresight and the tyranny of the majority". The Government is using its overwhelming majority to push its agenda through the House, something it is unable to do by acting in a democratic, proper and parliamentary way. They have thrown out the Standing Orders to achieve their objective.
The Government tells us that the situation is urgent and that passage of these Bills cannot be delayed. It brings up the issues of tax reform, free trade, abortion-there's an issue of great importance to the country, Mr. Speaker! We would like to resolve that issue, but the Government has neither the heart nor the courage nor the expertise to table a Bill. What does it want? It would like to table a motion, something lukewarm. We don't quite know what the government's intention is because it is incapable of leading the country or of proposing something concrete to the House. It would prefer to poll Members and when it has a clearer picture, to ask some legal experts to draft a Bill.
In the Globe and Mail,


Extension of Sittings
It is quoted. The Globe and Mail says that the Liberal Deputy Whip, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault), thunders that the Government is trying to do an opinion poll of Members of Parliament, an awful precedent. That is true. Government Members are. They are unable to make up their minds. They are unable to come forth with legislation. I believe they should be replaced. I believe this is wrong. This Government has absolutely lost control. It does not know what it is doing. It is now in a situation where it wants to push through everything in the hope that Canadians will buy that. Canadians will not buy that nonsense.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in opposition to Motion No. 26 that will extend the sittings of this House into the summer with extended sitting on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Thursdays. We see that this motion is being pushed through the House by closure. We can be sure that this is only the first of many attempts by the Government to ram things through the House in violation of the tenets of democracy.
I oppose this motion first of all personally. I oppose it because it interferes with my own personal agenda as a human being, and I think that is important.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext: It interferes with your vacation, 10 weeks.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext:
That is important because it disrupts my plans. It disrupts my plans for life with my family and it disrupts my plans to do things in my constituency. I might say that in my case my children are grown up, so it is not as important to me as it is to many other Members. The disruption of family life is very serious.
Second, unless the Government has enough guts to call an election in the next two or three weeks, I will not be running again. I have said quite plainly that I will not be running after redistribution, so I am not as involved as other Members are in election work.
This is a violation of the rights of Members to be able to plan their lives, their constituency work, and their family and vacation time so that there is a degree of rationality introduced into all this.
A few years ago we brought in parliamentary reform, putting an end to this whole business of vacation roulette, with both the Opposition and the Government playing games with vacations. This whole process-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext: It's like voting on first reading. Tell us what your constituents think about that.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext: You will get a chance to speak later. You had a chance to speak earlier after the Liberal Member. Why don't you shut up now and listen? You are not only trying to push this through on closure; you are not prepared to listen.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was trying to speak with some degree of rationality about parliamentary reform, and I will be addressing the Chair. You yourself, Mr. Speaker, know how important it was when parliamentary reform was introduced a few years ago. It meant that Members, both on the government side and the opposition side, could plan their lives with some degree of certainty. The Government has now tossed that out the window. It did it first last August by calling us back on a spurious refugee crisis. A boatload of Sikhs had arrived off the coast of Newfoundland.
It is interesting that just a week ago the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) indicated that the refugees he is really concerned about are existentialists. He is concerned about having a boatload of existentialists arrive off the coast of Vancouver Island. He is afraid that some nihilists or some people who believe in situational ethics will arrive. Those are the people the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta indicated Canada had to protect itself against when he spoke a week ago Friday. Perhaps you were here for that memorable event, Mr. Speaker.
In any event, we were all called back last August to deal with this so-called crisis. As you know, Mr. Speaker, there was no real crisis at all. Now, once again, we are throwing the parliamentary calendar out the window. We are throwing out any vestige of parliamentary reform that would let Members of Parliament plan their lives with any degree of certainty.
The Government is planning to use a platoon system. Government Members are not all planning to be here during summer sittings. In committee last week we were talking about a report, and the chairperson was very insistent that this report be tabled by June 28. I said: "Well, since the Government plans on having us here into July and August, why the rush?"
He said: "Well, I'm not going to be here; I'm not planning on being here". This is an abuse of the Government's majority. It has 208 Members to 72 opposition Members, though there will probably be 73 after today. The Government wants to abuse this system because government Members outnumber opposition Members by three to one, more or less. They think they can have one platoon here and another platoon out campaigning.
Of course, there are some pretty good candidates who are not Members of Parliament out there campaigning. They will do a number on those people for the abuse of democracy that this represents.
The Opposition has not been obstructionist in the House. The Hon. Member who spoke previously pointed out that we have passed a good number of Bills on a wide range of issues over the past number of months. Just this past Friday, the Opposition co-operated for speedy passage of Bill C-131 dealing with transportation for disabled people. Two weeks earlier, we co-operated by pushing through five different Bills


dealing with Indian affairs. We have co-operated on such things as tobacco legislation.
Whenever there is some issue with which we agree, we will give every bit of co-operation to the Government that we possibly can, even to the extent of forgoing making speeches on issues about which we feel very strongly. On issues to which we are opposed, we do not obstruct. We have degrees of opposition, as the Government knows. Sometimes we will put up only two or three speakers when we are opposed to a Bill. At other times we will put up more.
The one area in which we are quite firm and have said we are not going to let the Government push through is the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal. We oppose this with everything we have and every method at our disposal under the rules of Parliament because we see it as a sell-out of the Canadian people and a sell-out of Canadian sovereignty.
That is what this motion is all about. Motion No. 26 is really the attempt of the Government to push through Bill C-130 dealing with the trade deal. The Government has mismanaged its agenda which is so important to the Prime Minister and now wants to bring in extended days of sitting in order to push through Bill C-130 which was only introduced in this House on May 24. Everything about this trade deal illustrates an abuse of democratic process, and the motion to have extended sittings of this House is only the latest chapter in this abusive process.
You yourself, Mr. Speaker, were a delegate at the convention in 1983 at which the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) indicated that he was opposed to any trade deal with the United States. He said that the people of Canada opposed it in 1911 and would oppose it in 1983. In our Party we believe that the people of Canada will oppose this particular deal very strongly in 1988 when they finally get around to having an election.
In 1984, when the Prime Minister was campaigning across Canada, he campaigned on a program of opposing patronage, on honesty in government and things like that, but he did not campaign on having a trade deal with the United States. Far from it; he indicated that he was opposed.

You just didn't listen.
Mr. Manly. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary said that I did not listen. Extension of Sittings

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND SITTINGS
speechtext:
Yes, he is a Minister. Suddenly in 1985 we had an initiative to discuss this trade deal with the United States. For the next year and a half secret discussions were going on. The people of Canada were told very little of what was happening. The provinces were given only minimal information. The House of Commons was kept in the dark and when we were told anything we were not told the whole story.
I remember an opposition day debate on the trade agreement a year and some months ago. We wanted to know what was in that agreement. The then Minister for International Trade stood and said that she would tell us what was in the agreement, but she did not mention such things as the energy sell-out, which is such an important part of this deal. She never mentioned that although she was a former Minister of Energy and knew how important it was to the Canadian economy and the Canadian people.
Last fall over some Kentucky Fried Chicken there was a last minute agreement on the deal. The deal was cut as though by a used car salesman trying anything just to get a deal: "I'll throw in this, I'll throw in that; you give me this, I'll give you that". What a way to negotiate Canadian sovereignty.
Following that agreement we did not have the final text but only the elements of the agreement. There was a farce of committee hearings across Canada, one day in British Columbia and one day in each of the other provinces. We were not able to hear all the concerns of people about this matter. The people did not have the final text. It only arrived in the last couple of days before the committee had to report. The committee was under the gun. It was supposed to report before Christmas so that everything would be in order for the Prime Minister and President Reagan to sign on January 2. It was rushed through committee without giving the people of Canada an adequate chance to hear, to study, and to make their views known.
In Question Period we have seen the stonewalling of the Government on the questions which we have asked to try to get answers on what this deal is really all about. Instead of the Government coming forth and telling us what this is all about, we have a multimillion dollar deal to advertise it to the people of Canada, to try to sell it like soap. At the same time we have the refusal of a great many Tory Members of Parliament to debate the issue at the local level in local forums, to stand up with opponents of the deal and say what is right and what is wrong about it.
On May 24 the Government finally tabled Bill C-130, and now it wants to push it through. It is using Motion No. 26 to have extended hours and extended days of sitting to push through this ill-advised Bill which will spell the end of Canada's right to manage its own economy. It is a form of legislation by exhaustion.
When we agreed a number of years ago to parliamentary reform and a set parliamentary calendar, there was an element in the agreement which allowed for extended sittings in the last two weeks of June. That allows the Government to get a


lot of its business done and, at the same time, allows Members of Parliament to plan their schedules. The Government is now violating that agreement.
We will still have extended sittings during the last two weeks of June, and this creates some difficulty for the New Democrats with only 32 Members and the Liberals with only 40 Members trying to cover all bases. Elowever, we are prepared to accept that kind of limitation. We are not, however, prepared to accept this kind of legislation by exhaustion into July and August. This is reminiscent of the 1956 pipeline debate when C. D. Howe and Louis St. Laurent pushed the pipeline Bill through this House of Commons.
In four years the Conservative Government has grown as arrogant and as uncaring as the Liberals did in 1956 and 1957 after 22 years in power. I can assure them that when the Canadian people finally get a chance to vote on this issue the results will be exactly the same. Tory Ministers are as abusive of the rights of Parliament as were the Liberals in 1956.
Perhaps I could refer very briefly to the record of the Tories when they were in opposition in 1981 and to how strongly they opposed Liberal motions of closure. The Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the Minister who was going to be pushing this legislation through, said:
This comes from a closure-crazed government, a government which suffers from the crime of parliamentary bestiality. It cannot wait to force these kinds of things through the House.
Further he said:
The same little group comes in here on every closure motion. The same little group of parliamentary eunuchs-
I have some trouble with this mixed metaphor. On the one hand he talks about parliamentary bestiality and on the other he refers to a group of parliamentary eunuchs. Apart from that, he said:
-the same group of parliamentary assassins-are in here all the time, assassinating this House and removing the good from the House. That is why I call them the parliamentary eunuchs. The good has already been removed from them.
Perhaps I could call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and finish my remarks after Question Period.

subtopic: SHORTAGE OF QUALIFIED LABOUR
SHORTAGE OF QUALIFIED LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business advises that 42 per cent of its 80,000 member firms report a shortage of qualified labour and that in about half of these the cause was a lack of qualified skills. The irony is that at the same time a million Canadians are unemployed. The newspapers of the nation carry pages of advertisements of jobs available while Governments spend billions of dollars on discretionary grants to businesses and organizations.
Why all these apparent contradictions? Is it because Governments and business are asking for unnecessary qualifications such as bilingualism when only one language is required, or is it a lack of basics in the three R's? Whatever the reasons, it is high time that a review as recommended by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration is carried out. Surely such a review will recommend that some of the government grants be allocated to


upgrading basics under the job development and re-entry programs.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
subtopic: NEED FOR SIMPLIFIED FORMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Concise Oxford Dictionary defines "simplify" as meaning to "make simple, make easy or easier to do or understand".
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) talked about tax reform he said it would also include tax simplification, that is, he would make it easier for Canadians to understand and fill out their tax forms.
Earlier this year he brought out the new TD1 form that every Canadian who receives an income must fill out. In my riding of Thunder Bay-Atikokan I was recently told of a pensioner who receives a tiny sum each month by way of a private pension. We are talking about $10 a month, hardly enough to pay for bus fare let alone pay tax. However, under the Minister of Finance's new tax reform, this pensioner is still required to fill out this new form consisting of no fewer than 16 questions. This is tax reform? This is a simplified tax form?
I suggest that the Hon. Minister, if he wants to make taxes easier to do, apply a little commonsense to the process. Either that or he should read the dictionary before he uses words that have more than two syllables.

OPENING OF MOOSE JAW MULTICULTURAL COUNCIL'S PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was my pleasure to participate in the opening of a park in Moose Jaw yesterday afternoon. Happy Valley is a new picnic ground in an area of the city that was once residential but was abandoned because of occasional flooding during spring run-off.
This project was unusual because it was arranged and brought to its present stage with very little funding by either the federal, provincial or municipal level of government.
The sponsoring body of this project is the Moose Jaw Multicultural Council. At the opening ceremonies, flags from the homelands of the various ethnic groups that are members were proudly flying in the breeze.
I salute the hardworking president, Mr. Rudy Namtu, and all members of the council for this very worth-while project. I would also like to recognize the students of Ross School who assisted in the planting of hundreds of trees this past spring.
I am sure this example could be followed in many communities across Canada.

DISTRIBUTION OF COOKIES MADE WITH IRRADIATED FLOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Atomic Energy of Canada has become the cookie monster. But unlike its Sesame Street counterpart, AECL does not hoard cookies, it gives them out freely.
This publicly funded body is distributing chocolate chip cookies made with irradiated flour. Why chocolate chip cookies you may ask? Think about it. How much irradiated liver could one give away?
Some recipients of these treats have discovered that if the cookies are not eaten right away, and left in the light for a week, they turn bone coloured. If they are stored in the darkness, the cookies still become a light tan colour. Some were afraid that irradiated products would glow in the dark. Now it appears they are whitening with daylight.
The reason for irradiation is allegedly to enhance the food's longevity in storage. Grandma's chocolate chip cookies never lasted beyond a few hours before they were eaten. Perhaps irradiation does overcome that problem.

STUDY'S FUNDINGS OF EFFECT ON DISPOSABLE INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have seen once again today that the Tory idea of tax reform is to let the rich pay less and the poor pay more. As a result of Tory tax reform, the average family in Canada earning between $29,000 and $35,000 a year, is actually losing about $680 in disposable income. MATHEMATICS USED IN CALCULATING SERVICE FEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, service fee charges continue to multiply. However, it is now the banks and trust companies charging each other with having the highest service fees.
It is obvious that over the past few years both banks and trust companies have become very proficient at subtraction as they take money out of customers' accounts more and more frequently. However, the question raised last week is whether they can add. A real division now exists over which institution is subtracting the most from customer accounts.
My initial reaction was that they needed a higher form of mathematics, for example, differential calculus, to settle the dispute by calculating the velocity at which money is leaving customers' accounts. However, even differential calculus appears inadequate to settle this issue.
Only the most advanced calculus, residue theory, is adequate to settle this issue once and for all. For those not familiar with residue theory it is also used in calculations involving material close to an unlimited black hole in space.
Perhaps the banks and trust companies will cancel their charges at least against each other if not against consumers, and refer the dispute to the universities.

Mr. Speaker, my private views on the railway are the same as my public views which have been known for months. They are that any question of abandoning the railway ought to involve, first, recognition of our rights under the Terms of Union and proper compensation, not accounted for today. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into transportation of 1978 said that the federal Government should be required to ensure that sufficient funds are available to maintain the entire Trans-Canada Highway in the province and also to increase port facilities. It recommended as well that this maintenance money ought to be provided in perpetuity, as it is now provided in the case of the railway. In fact, we will have $6.6 million per year for 15 years and then we are on our own.
The Deputy Prime Minister knows my private views. He now knows my public views. Why have those reasonable conditions which this Party adheres to, and which the Leader of this Party publicly endorsed in St. John's, Newfoundland,


Oral Questions
not been met in the agreement signed today? What kind of chicanery is the Government involved in in trying to rip off the poorest of all the provinces of Canada with this agreement signed today in Newfoundland?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ROYAL COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not a rip-off and the Hon. Member knows it. If the Hon. Member reads Article 31 and Article 32 of the Terms of Union, he will find that the undertakings that were made at that time are being in fact fulfilled in this announcement by the Government of Canada. Furthermore, there was also a provision to guarantee some protection with respect to freight rates. That too has been included in this package.
We are getting a lot of rhetoric here, and a bit of fanfare coming from the Hon. Member. I think that on reflection, when he studies the package thoroughly, he will find out that this is done in the best interests of Newfoundland.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: FUNDING OF TRANS-LABRADOR HIGHWAY

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
subtopic: FUNDING OF TRANS-LABRADOR HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. In 1978 the Hon. Member for St. John's West called Otto Lang an ogre, untrustworthy and heartless. However, Otto Lang built the airstrips along the Labrador coast and started the Trans-Labrador Highway.
Why is it that only $16 million has been allocated to that Trans-Labrador Highway in spite of the fact that the Sullivan Royal Commission recommended, if the railway was closed down, that a highway be built across Labrador? Why is it that Labrador is being treated as second class in this compensation package? Why is Labrador being sold out?
Judas Iscariot got 30 pieces of silver, and adding inflation that is more than we got today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FUNDING OF TRANS-LABRADOR HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under this agreement Labrador is not being sold out, neither is Newfoundland being sold out. The people of Labrador and of Newfoundland are not being sold out. Transportation services will be provided in the future.
As a matter of fact, the steps that are being taken here will build for the future and will provide the kind of competitive transportation system that will in fact enhance the economic opportunities for Newfoundland and Labrador. I think the Hon. Member recognizes that. The fact is that the road network will be improved. That is something that the Newfoundland Government believes is desirable and that is something that the people of Newfoundland believe is desirable. The Hon. Member will have an excellent transportation system that will handle people and goods.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: OBSERVANCE OF CONSTITUTIONAL OBLIGATIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
subtopic: OBSERVANCE OF CONSTITUTIONAL OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I asked the Deputy Prime
Minister if the Government of Canada would live up to its constitutional obligations, and he said yes, it would, as reported in Hansard. Today we have seen that the Government of Canada has failed to live up to those constitutional obligations.
Those obligations require the Government of Canada to maintain a transportation system at national standards across the province, not just Newfoundland but across the province. That has failed to be done. Why did the Deputy Prime Minister say in the House a week ago that he would live up to the constitutional obligations of 1949 but today the Government has sold out the province so cheaply? Why?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: OBSERVANCE OF CONSTITUTIONAL OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member, on reflection, may want to restudy that point because the fact is that Article 31 and Article 32 of the Terms of Union have been lived up to and fulfilled, as has the commitment to provide some protection for freight rates. That, too, has been incorporated in the agreement. I would invite the Hon. Member to re-examine the agreement. He will find that that is the case.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS
PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. In view of the well known policies of the Government to privatize, deregulate, close down, and abandon the public services of Canada, it should come as no surprise to Newfoundlanders today to hear that the Government is going to close down the Newfoundland Railway.
The people of Newfoundland want to know today why their province alone has to put up with the abandonment of constitutional rights as spelled out in the agreement, that is, that this agreement and the funds are offered in full satisfaction of all Canada's constitutional obligations related to railways on the island of Newfoundland.
Why is Newfoundland, of all provinces in Canada, required to give up its constitutional rights in order to get a decent road system?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, the Terms of Union are being lived up to.

subtopic: PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS
speechtext: You bought them for a few baubles.

subtopic: PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS
speechtext: Shut up.

subtopic: PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS
speechtext: I won't shut up. Try and shut me up.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS
speechtext: Order. The Hon. Minister has the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
As I said, Mr. Speaker, Articles 31 and 32 are in fact being lived up to as is the commitment to provide some guarantee and protection for freight rates.


The objective of the Government has been, is, and will continue to be to provide better transportation services to more Canadians from coast to coast. I think the record clearly speaks for itself in terms of the overhaul of the National Transportation Act, improved air services, and the more competitive nature of our transportation system.
Doing this will provide a better opportunity for more Canadians from coast to coast to take advantage of the economic opportunities available through an enhanced transportation system. That is the objective and the reasoning behind this agreement which is supported by the Government of the Province of Newfoundland, by workers, and by many people who live in the affected communities of Newfoundland.
I invite the Hon. Member to re-examine the arrangement in order to see the positive benefits which will flow from this very good agreement which has been negotiated by the two levels of government.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: AMOUNT OF FEDERAL FUNDING
AMOUNT OF FEDERAL FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 1987 Newfoundland Royal Commission on Employment and Unemployment concluded that it would require $64 million a year, $40 million of which ought to be indexed to inflation, in perpetuity in order to compensate the people of Newfoundland for the loss of the railway. That is in addition to the requirements of compensating the 500 Newfoundlanders who will lose their jobs as a result of this.
This agreement provides for about $700 million over 15 years for transportation, only about $50 million a year, and nothing after that. Why are the people of Newfoundland being ripped off by the Government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMOUNT OF FEDERAL FUNDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the people of Newfoundland are not being ripped off by the Government. We are putting in place a program for an improved transportation service which will allow Newfoundlanders and the people of Labrador to take better advantage of the economic opportunities available to them. The Hon. Member should be applauding that rather than ridiculing it.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION
GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister said that this agreement is supported by the workers. Well, all the workers are getting under this agreement is what they are already entitled to under agreements they themselves have negotiated over the last number of years. They are getting nothing from the Government over and above that. The railway is being closed down September 1, 1988, but there will be no money spent on the TransCanada highway until 1992.
Why is the Government taking advantage of the unfortunate economic situation of the Government of Newfoundland and forcing it to accept this agreement and give up its rights for
Oral Questions
inadequate compensation? Why does the Government not deal fairly with the people of Newfoundland?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is wrong when he suggests that the federal Government is taking advantage of the people of Newfoundland. This agreement has been negotiated-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: The Government is looking for a few bucks to try to win an election.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Order. The Hon. Minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: This agreement was negotiated with the Government of Newfoundland after extensive consultation. Such consultations have been going on for years. The agreement is put forth in the best interests of Newfoundland with the best opportunities for it to enhance its economic opportunities and have a first-class, up-to-date, efficient, safe, and competitive transportation system for the future.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: EFFECT ON NORTH SYDNEY, N. S.
EFFECT ON NORTH SYDNEY, N. S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is likewise for the Deputy Prime Minister. If this is a stab in the back of the Province of Newfoundland, it is a stab in the heart of the Town of North Sydney. The Government has at least made a pretence of compensating the Province of Newfoundland and Newfoundlanders, but it has not given one cent to Cape Bretoners who will be losing their jobs as a result of this railway closure.
Why does the Government not admit that it is going to be devastating the economy of the town of North Sydney and costing the people of North Sydney jobs? Why does the Government not at least have the courage to admit that this is only the first step in the closure of the railway in Nova Scotia between Truro and Sydney?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EFFECT ON NORTH SYDNEY, N. S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is categorically wrong in that assumption. The fact of the matter is that CN will continue to maintain rail service to North Sydney. At the moment trains between Truro and Sydney have an average of 80 to 90 cars per day. The fact is that we will still have a multi-modal transportation service in this area.
As the Hon. Member knows, CN has probably one of the most generous and comprehensive adjustment, retirement, and retraining programs of any corporation in Canada. I am sure that he will be most helpful to his constituents in ensuring that if there is any adjustment he will be there to assist them, as will I.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL LAY-OFFS
CANADIAN NATIONAL LAY-OFFS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what the Deputy Prime Minister is saying is the most insidious thing I have heard in this House of Commons in a


Oral Questions
long, long time. If there is to be no problem in Cape Breton why are four CN workers being laid off as of July 21? Why are two more being laid off as of the middle of September?
Why does the Deputy Prime Minister not then commit right now that there will be no rail closure of the line between Truro and Sydney? Will he guarantee right now that that line will remain open and that there will be no job losses in industrial Cape Breton?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL LAY-OFFS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is talking about adjustment and protection for the workers. There is a $75 million labour adjustment and related expenditure program as a result of this announcement. There is a $15 million community adjustment program and an $8.2 million development program for ports.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL LAY-OFFS
speechtext: The ports are in Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL LAY-OFFS
speechtext: There is a $62 million ERDA agreement.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL LAY-OFFS
speechtext: There is nothing for Cape Breton.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL LAY-OFFS
speechtext: This is in addition to the very generous employee benefits of the CNR.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL LAY-OFFS
speechtext: Your nose is growing.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL LAY-OFFS
speechtext: The Member knows that. The fact of the matter, which the Member conveniently overlooks, is that the massive lay-offs which took place before 1984 make the adjustment which may occur now very miniscule by nature. He sat there and did absolutely nothing about them.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: WORKERS' SEVERANCE PAY-EFFECT ON ELIGIBILITY FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: WORKERS' SEVERANCE PAY-EFFECT ON ELIGIBILITY FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for the unemployment insurance program. It was announced today that the Newfoundland Railway will be closed on September 1, 1988. The workers were never involved in the negotiations and were, in fact, informed at eight o'clock this morning of the deal. They will all be out of jobs on September 1, 1988, and their severance packages will not allow them to collect unemployment insurance. Because the unemployment insurance program was changed by this Government severance pay and all other remuneration they will receive will be applied to benefits.
Can the Minister stand up and tell me whether we are going to punish Newfoundland railway workers three times?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
subtopic: WORKERS' SEVERANCE PAY-EFFECT ON ELIGIBILITY FOR UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unemployment insurance exists to help workers who become entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. This Government has created programs to assist the social reintegration of the unemployed. Under the
specific programs like the one mentioned by the Hon. Member, we have allocated special funding on a shared-cost basis with industry, and we intend to do everything we can to ensure that the dignity of the Canadian worker is respected.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER CHANGE ELIGIBILITY REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER CHANGE ELIGIBILITY REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to September, 1984, severance pay and any other emoluments paid to workers when they lost their jobs through no fault of their own were never considered income for unemployment insurance purposes. It was the present Government that made that change and discriminated against unemployed workers.
There are no provisions in the unemployment insurance program to give benefits to workers. It will be mostly older workers who will be affected. They will never be able to get a job as quickly as when they were younger.
Will the Minister tell the House if she is prepared at least to go back and change the regulations so that any unfairness of this sort will be eliminated?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER CHANGE ELIGIBILITY REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I repeat that unemployment insurance exists for people who are looking for a job, for people who are laid off, and that is why this Government has created programs to assist social reintegration, and we intend to continue creating jobs at the same rate we have maintained since 1984.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: EFFECT OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT ON NEWFOUNDLAND
EFFECT OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT ON NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today will go down in the books as a dark day for Newfoundland because Newfoundland becomes the only province in Canada without a railway. I am wondering why.
Why is Newfoundland the only province in Canada that is forced to give up its railway, with hundreds of permanent employees, in exchange for some money to upgrade its roads? Quebec did not have to give up its railway when the Prime Minister announced $900 million two weeks ago to upgrade its roads. Why is Newfoundland the only province in Canada that is forced to trade rails for roads?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EFFECT OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT ON NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this agreement was not forced upon the people of Newfoundland or the Government of Newfoundland. It was negotiated with the Government of Newfoundland which speaks on behalf of the people of Newfoundland. It was negotiated very simply because it was considered to be in the best long term interests of the people of Newfoundland, with economic development and a good transportation system so that Newfoundlanders


can have the same opportunities as people in every other part of Canada. That is why the deal was negotiated.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: EFFECT ON FREIGHT TRANSPORTATION
EFFECT ON FREIGHT TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not the closure of a branch of a railway or a portion of a railway, this is the closure of the entire 960 kilometres of the railway in exchange for 166 kilometres of pavement. That is only 18 per cent of the entire Trans-Canada Highway in Newfoundland.
Does the Minister really believe that Newfoundlanders will believe this is a fair deal? Does the Minister not realize that as a result of this deal every single bit of freight that crosses Newfoundland will have to go on that road? This includes all the dangerous substances, explosives, dangerous chemicals, the whole shebang will have to go over that one road with only 166 kilometres of new pavement.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EFFECT ON FREIGHT TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Member is such an advocate of the railway why did he not get out and campaign with the shippers and the producers of Newfoundland to get them to utilize the railway? Quite frankly, the fact of the matter is that traffic volumes have declined to such an extent that it is totally non economic to continue the operation. Rather than pouring more money into the support of that operation it was considered to be more effective to build a better transportation infrastructure which would allow Newfoundlanders to take full advantage of the economic opportunities that are available to them.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: MILITARY COUP D'ETAT IN HAITI-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Our hopes and the hopes of Haitians that democracy would come to Haiti have been dashed by a military coup and by statements made by General Namphy, to the effect that he will establish a non-democratic, military junta. Four of Haiti's major donor countries are at the Summit in Toronto. Has the Canadian Government raised this issue so that these governments can prepare an effective response?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: MILITARY COUP D'ETAT IN HAITI-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to answer on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and to inform the Hon. Member that we are monitoring the situation very closely. The issue was indeed raised at the Summit in Toronto, and we will have news about the discussions on the present situation in Haiti very shortly.
Oral Questions

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: QUERY WHETHER CANADA WILL RECEIVE PRESIDENT MANIGAT AS REFUGEE
QUERY WHETHER CANADA WILL RECEIVE PRESIDENT MANIGAT AS REFUGEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there were some rumours to the effect that Mr. Manigat plans to come to Canada to seek asylum. Is this true? What would the Canadian Government's response be to his request?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: QUERY WHETHER CANADA WILL RECEIVE PRESIDENT MANIGAT AS REFUGEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a very hypothetical question. Of course, when we have a situation like the present one in Haiti, Canada is always mentioned as a possibility. At the present time, however, we cannot assume that the deposed president is now actually on his way to Canada. We will have to follow the same immigration rules that all other people have to follow when they want to come here. However, it is all very hypothetical at this time.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT JUSTIFY POLICY OF PRECEDING 10 MONTHS
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT JUSTIFY POLICY OF PRECEDING 10 MONTHS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. After the coup, it was obvious that General Namphy would once again proclaim himself to be Haiti's Head of State. This is the same gentleman for whom the Canadian Conservative Government had high hopes, the same gentleman the Canadian ambassador trusted so implicitly. The Parliamentary Secretary must be pretty embarrassed on behalf of his Government today! I want to ask him how, in the light of recent events, he can justify the Conservative Government's lack of coherence in its policy visa-vis Haiti during the past year or so.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT JUSTIFY POLICY OF PRECEDING 10 MONTHS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very much surprised to hear the Hon. Member qualify a situation we are analysing as events unfold as being perfectly obvious. I find it even more surprising since Canada's policy will be affected, especially by the unanimous report we tabled, a report to which the Hon. Member was a party. As far as the assistance program is concerned, what is now happening in Haiti merely reinforces our position, and we have no reason to be embarrassed. I would refer the Hon. Member to statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the House in which he expressed considerable reservations about the electoral process. We did not say we recognized this or that president. We recognized a State. In fact, this was made clear in our initial recommendation that Canada should maintain the present level of its diplomatic representation in Haiti. I signed that report, Mr. Speaker, and the Hon. Member opposite signed as well, and I believe our report remains relevant. The people of Haiti need help.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: SAFETY OF CANADIANS IN HAITI-GOVERNMENT POSITION
SAFETY OF CANADIANS IN HAITI-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what the Haitian people need above all is democracy, real democracy. I want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary what kind of concrete
COMMONS DEBATES___________________June 20, 1988
Oral Questions
measures the Canadian Government will consider to support the upright citizens who wish to create a democracy in Haiti. And especially, I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary whether he can give the House the assurance today that the safety of Canadians working in Haiti, and I am thinking especially of missionaries, is assured at this time. Are the people who had the courage to ask publicly for democracy in Haiti threatened today by this dictator who has just come back to power, and what will the Conservative Government do to help Canadian nationals who may be at risk today in Haiti?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SAFETY OF CANADIANS IN HAITI-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, reports received from Port-au-Prince, from our ambassador who is still posted there, indicate there is no danger to Canadians at the present time. Of course, since it is an emergency situation, we must always analyse events as they unfold, and the Department of External Affairs is constantly in touch with our ambassador in Haiti. We are analysing the situation, and as in other instances when difficult situations arise, we will be able to take steps as required to protect the lives of Canadians who are in Haiti and who are doing humanitarian work and a magnificent job.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES-TOTAL COST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. Today we learned that Rear Admiral John Anderson, who heads the Minister's own nuclear submarine acquisition program, has indicated that the Minister's $8 billion price tag for the nuclear attack submarines fails to include a number of critical components, including ship-to-shore communication systems, the missiles that will be used on the ships, the cost of making nuclear fuel and a whole range of items.
As the Deputy Prime Minister well knows, when a Canadian goes in to buy a car, that individual wants to know what the full cost will be before he signs on the dotted line. Before the Minister of National Defence signs on the dotted line and locks Canadian taxpayers into a multibillion dollar package, would it not be appropriate to know what the actual total cost is before he makes that commitment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES-TOTAL COST
speechtext:
Indeed it would, Mr. Speaker, and indeed we do. There are a number
of elements in the Hon. Member's question that are simply false. For example, it is not our intention to acquire anti-ship missiles. Were we to do so, however, they would replace the Mark 48 torpedo we are buying for the submarines and an anti-ship torpedo would cost less money than a Mark 48 torpedo. Is the Hon. Member suggesting we should do that? If he is, we would actually be saving money.
Second, with respect to fuel fabrication, we do not intend to fabricate it in Canada although we will have the ability to load the fuel in Canada-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES-TOTAL COST
speechtext: You are going to buy it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES-TOTAL COST
speechtext: -and that is included in the $8 billion figure. Third, with respect to the VLF communications with the submarines, these submarines will be capable, as are our three Oberon Class submarines today, of receiving these messages. At the present time we use allied communications systems. We have taken no decision on whether to build our own or to continue to use allied communications systems. If we do, we would take that into consideration and it would come off the $8 billion figure.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES-TOTAL COST
speechtext: Perhaps what the Minister of National Defence should do is sit down with Rear Admiral John Anderson and explain to him that, although he heads the Minister's own nuclear submarine Hunter Attack Submarine Task Force, he obviously does not know what he is talking about. One or the other is not being straight with the people of Canada.

subtopic: PRICE QUERY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to direct my supplementary question to the Minister of National Defence. In terms of the acquisition of nuclear fuel, can the Minister tell us what the actual price tag will be, the price tag for the actual purchase of the updated communications system, the price tag for the missiles that will be used, the price tag for the new port facilities, which are not included, and the price tag for the training of the crews, which have not been factored in? Will the Minister now simply be honest and straightforward with the people of Canada and tell them precisely what the price tag per sub will be?

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was speaking to Motion No. 26 which will extend the sitting of the House into the summer with extended hours. Our contention, of course, is that the Government wants this motion in order that it can force through Bill C-130 which puts into place the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal. The Government is using this legislation by exhaustion to force upon the people of Canada a piece of legislation for which the Government has no mandate. Instead of pushing this legislation through the Government should call an election.
1 urge the Government to reconsider its whole approach to this legislation. The Progressive Conservatives have a proud record in opposition of opposing this type of imposition of law through closure. They are trying to push through Motion No. 26 today by closure. In 1956 the Progressive Conservatives stood very strongly against the imposition of closure by the Liberal Government of Louis St. Laurent. In the Trudeau years the Conservatives were very strong against the Government's use of closure. As I quoted earlier in my speech, the Progressive Conservatives used inflammatory language, speaking of jackboot democracy and so on. Now, when they are on the other side of the House, they are using exactly the same tactics.
I ask government Members to reconsider their approach. They will be in opposition soon enough themselves. They will regret the fact that they have thrown the whole parliamentary calendar, the whole business of parliamentary reform, into the ashcan for the sake of a very short-term advantage in the


Extension of Sittings
House where they can use their parliamentary majority to push through legislation on which, that by rights, the people of Canada should have an election before it comes to the House.
I urge the Government to reconsider the importance of the parliamentary calendar to individual Members, to Members who have families, from the point of view of democracy as a whole. We want intelligent people to be able to stand for office. When intelligent people look at the manner in which this Government is demeaning the process of democracy, having a process of legislation by exhaustion, having a process by which individual Members of Parliament are denied the right to be with their families during the summer, they will simply say: "This is not for me".
I urge the Government to consider the fact that it will be in opposition itself and will not want this type of precedent to be forced back on it, to consider its own history of opposition to this type of jackboot tactics, and to consider the basic process of democracy. If it does that, I am sure it will withdraw this motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of State and Minister of State (Treasury Board)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak because I had made a speech in proposing the motion. However, I have been moved by the "Government is bungling everything" speech of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) and the "I want to get to the swimming pool" speech of the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly).
I want to say that we did not bring in closure without a great deal of thought. In fact, we regret the necessity to close this debate, but here is the situation with which we were faced, and I wish to refer you, Mr. Speaker, to the Debates of last week.
On Monday of last week from 11 a.m. until 1 p.m. the House was delayed by the delaying tactics of the NDP. When one of their Members moved to introduce a Bill, half the Party said "yea" and the other half said "nay" and thus forced a vote. They did the same thing with respect to the question on whether or not the Bill should be printed. Unfortunately, that was a Bill to confer on Raoul Wallenberg honorary Canadian citizenship. We objected at the time, as did the Liberal Party, to the NDP playing politics with that very important matter.
On Wednesday of last week from 3 p.m. until 6 p.m. the House Leader of the New Democratic Party introduced two Private Members' Bills, forcing votes on the introduction and forcing votes on first reading, thus delaying away the entire day.
On Thursday of last week it was a short day because of the speech by Helmut Kohl, Chancellor of West Germany. The NDP did the same thing and delayed so that the whole day was wasted.
Thus Members of the New Democratic Party wasted two full days and one-half day last week. They now come in here
and talk about legislation by exhaustion. They cannot have it both ways. If they delay and delay and do not allow for debate, then one cannot say: "Well, we are not getting our opportunity to debate".
My hon. friend from Ottawa-Vanier said that we should have moved earlier last week to do today what we did. I want to refer my friend to the precedent in this matter which occurred back in April of 1987. I want to refer my hon. friend from Ottawa-Vanier to some of the comments of the Speaker when he made his ruling that it was within the rules to move, during Routine Proceedings, that the House move to Orders of the Day.
The Speaker made reference to the fact that the fundamental rights of Members can be violated by the tactics of obstruction as well as by unreasonable restriction of debate. He said that sooner or later every issue must be decided, and that the decision will be taken by a majority. The point to remember from the Speaker's decision is this. He said that he did not make the decision with a great deal of joy, and that the decision was made in such a way that if Member's wished to refer to it in the future, and if it was to be resorted to as a precedent, then the Chair will interpret it in the light of prevailing circumstances with a view to maintaining the essential balance to which the Chair referred earlier in its decision.
The reason we did not do this last week was to give members of the Opposition an opportunity to see if they had made their point by delay and delay and delay, by not allowing the House to do anything. Obviously, they had not made their point. We just did not feel that it was appropriate to waste any more time of the House. They wasted two and a half days last week. We felt that the circumstances were there to bring into effect what the Speaker said was a precedent that cannot be abused.
We allowed for the delay last week. When the time of the House was being abused, that is when we brought in the motion to move to Orders of the Day.
My friend from Ottawa-Vanier quoted at length from the first letter of a series, that is, the letter of May 31, which I wrote to the two Opposition House Leaders. He took great glee in referring to the large number of pieces of legislation that were referred to in that letter, some of which-and this is admitted-had not even been introduced on the Order Paper. What my hon. friend forgot to talk about, which I will do for him now, is the letter of June 9 from myself to the Opposition House Leader.

There are also some four other Bills which, as was pointed out by my hon. friend, the House Leader of the Liberal Party, would not take a great deal of debate. We added five Bills which we felt we had to have before the House rose for the summer. I think it is fair to say that we have had a great deal of progress to this point.
My hon. friend from Ottawa-Vanier then went on to talk about the delay in passing Bill C-55 and Bill C-84. We have had those Bills out of this House for some time. Yes, we came back last August because of the emergency situation created by the arrival of a boatload of so-called refugees who did not want to go through the normal procedures. We moved to correct that abuse.
The abuse has shifted from the boat landing on the shore of Nova Scotia to the Senate of Canada. Bill C-84 has been delayed and delayed and delayed by the Senate. Bill C-55 has been delayed and delayed and delayed by the Senate. That is from where the delay is coming. We have acted to correct those problems, but the delay is coming from the Senate. If my hon. friend from Ottawa-Vanier wonders why those Bills have not passed, he need only raise on Wednesday that matter in the Liberal caucus, which after all is controlled by Senators, to see if he cannot try to free up the log-jam.
I want to review briefly some of the reasons we are bringing this motion to extend the sittings, so that we can put them in the perspective of what has happened since we originally brought in the motion and discussed this matter with Opposition House Leaders. I pointed out in my original remarks that we were on track with our agenda despite comments to the contrary by the Opposition. I pointed out that we were well ahead in our plans-

On a motion every Member of the House has 20 minutes to put his or her case. On a Bill speeches are restricted to a maximum of 10 minutes after eight hours of debate.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: Unanimous consent can change those rules. We could have 20 minutes for everybody on a Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: My hon. friend is now talking about unanimous consent. He now has a different idea. The Opposition objects mostly to the free vote.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING

Is it in the first paragraph of the manifesto that thou shalt have 10 weeks' vacation? My hon. friend better go back to his riding. He will find that most people who work in his riding do not get 10 weeks' vacation.

opposition Parties had not delayed. We intend to allow this debate to progress and then we will have a vote.
As I indicated to the House, tomorrow we will start with the very important issue of the free trade Bill, Bill C-130.
