I want to do a little better preparation. But I have a proposition, Mr. Speaker.
I come from a steel working town where people work on shifts. I know what the Tories have up their sleeves. They have already developed a roster system. At any given time in the House one-third of the Tory Members are here and two-thirds are off travelling the country and on vacation. I will move a proposition that, sure, we will sit for extended hours. We will sit all summer. We will work as hard as anybody, but the Tories who are not here should not pick up a paycheque. The 70 people here will be holding the can for 140 others who will be off playing and on vacation.

-the work of 28 committees, the work across the country of political Parties. In the meantime we have tried to create make-work projects for tired Conservatives who have had nothing to do. Right now I have been making quorum for the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare because there is not a Tory in the list of Tory members of the committee who is interested in coming on a consistent basis to


the standing committee. We in the Opposition have been making quorum for one of the most important committees.
We are certainly prepared to work and do our share, but we are sick and tired of watching 140 Tories running around the country on vacation, leaving only 70 people here at a given point in time. Let us call a spade a spade and let us call a Tory a Tory. Let us start looking at the voting and attendance records of Members. There are Conservative Members from the Hamilton area, Conservative Members who were elected in the last election, who will be "de-elected" in the next election and who have never spoken in the House or, if they have, it has been once or twice.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
There have been members of the Opposition who have been working day and night on committee, in the House, and with respect to other commitments to their political Parties and to to the people of Canada across the country. It is very easy for the Conservatives to say that they want to sit all summer because they have a roster system. At any given time two-thirds of the Tories are not in the House of Commons. Let us call a spade a spade and say that those two-thirds of Tories who are out of the Commons at any given point in time will have their paycheques cut by two-thirds. Why should we be paying Tories who are off gallivanting in swimming pools in their areas? Let us move a motion to cut their paycheques by two-thirds. I will support it. I am prepared to sit here and do the work of the House of Commons. I cannot stand the hypocrisy of the Government which claims that the Opposition does not want to work. We want to debate substantive issues. All the Government wants to do is ram through legislation.
Let us look at the so-called tax reform document that the Government wants to put through immediately. With one sweep of the hand, we are supposed to pass this legislation. Let me read just one little passage from the 500-page document to which the Parliament of Canada has not had an opportunity to give its full attention. This is the definition of an individual:
For the purposes of subsection (5), an individual shall be deemed to have
supported a person in a particular month of a taxation year if
Extension of Sittings
(a)	the person is a child of, or is dependent for support in the particular month on, the individual or the individual's spouse; and
(b)	where the individual is married at the end of the particular month,
(i)	the individual's income for the year (computed without reference to subsection (5) and section 63) exceeds that of the individual's spouse; and
(ii)	the individual's spouse was not, by reason of a breakdown of the marriage, living separate and apart from the individual at the end of the particular month and for a period of at least 90 days commencing in the year.
(7) For the purposes of subsection (5), where an allowance referred to in that subsection is paid in respect of a person for a particular month of a taxation year and no amount in respect of the allowance would, but for this subsection, be included in computing the income for the year of any individual, the individual to whom the allowance is paid shall be deemed to have supported the person in the particular month."
That is the simplified tax Bill. This is page 94 of the English version of this 500-page document. Yet the Government has introduced a package of legislation including the trade Bill, the abortion legislation, and the tax reform legislation. It says that Parliament should pass it, or the Government will try to hammer us by sitting day and night.
Government Members are not interested in quality debate. They are not interested in a real examination of the substance of tax reform. They are interested in ramming through a bunch of Bills because they intend to break the Opposition down through fatigue.
Let us consider the tax reform Bill alone. I believe that the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) has done a tremendous job in mobilizing the small business community to point out some of the loopholes and inadequacies of this particular legislation.

Mr. Speaker, we can say about automobile expenses alone . . .

Small business people in Canada are extremely concerned about changes which relate to automobile expenses. In fact, a number of groups has come before the Finance Committee to point out the inconsistencies in the legislation that is supposed to be rammed through by the end of this month.

And we can say, for example, that the groups that appeared before the Finance Committee all found these new rules very complex. The so-called simplification of the tax system is not really that, Mr. Speaker. Even the experts cannot understand it. Not just the factory worker in my riding, but even lawyers and chartered accountants cannot understand the "simplified" tax system proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the best illustration of this complexity was provided by the Joint Committee on Taxation of the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants. Here is what they said about the May 1988 tax reform: "As regards automobile expenses and related benefits, the draft legislation is terribly complex. It required 30


Extension of Sittings
different amendments to the Act and Regulations to translate into legal terms the measures proposed in the White Paper as later amended in December 1987. These provisions are full of technical errors, which proves that the writers themselves had great difficulty understanding the rules."

We are not simply talking about the false proposition of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that this is a simpler process. We are also talking about the technical errors which exist because the Government is intending to ram through this legislation with about 20 or 30 other pieces of legislation in the next couple of weeks. The Government is threatening that if we do not buckle under, if we do not cave in, it will pull the plug and we will sit day and night. Government Members do not care about the quality of tax reform legislation. All they want to do is stick it to the taxpayers.
The Institute for Research on Public Policy makes it very clear that as a a result of so-called Tory tax reform average taxpayers will be paying more, depending upon their income levels. If they are earning between $29,000 and $35,000, they will be losing, over the course of the Tory mandate, almost $700 in purchasing power. If their income is in the neighbourhood of $35,000 to $40,000 per year, they will actually be losing close to $900.
The only people who gain and gain substantially as a result of the so-called tax reform are the big buck earners who earn over $117,000 a year. How can the Minister claim that we should pass this legislation without giving a fair shake to the ordinary steelworking men and women of my riding who want to know why they are now paying more in taxes?
Some of these Members have been silent for four years. I was very happy to hear the Member from Toronto rise today to talk about the tax on building materials. Where was that Hon. Member when the first Tory Budget introduced a tax on building materials at the federal level? Where was that Hon. Member when this Minister introduced a plan to cut out the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan? Where was that Hon. Member when the same Government doubled insurance fees for CMHC from 1.5 per cent to 3 per cent on average adding hundreds, if not more than $1,000, to the cost of purchasing a home? I did not hear that Hon. Member complaining about a tax on building materials. He sat silently. Now he and his colleagues are involved in a conspiracy to try to convince Canadian taxpayers that we do not want to do the work of the House of Commons.
What we want is fair tax reform. We do not want to have the kind of tax reform that will tell ordinary taxpayers that they will have to pay an extra $1,200 as a result of the tax reforms of the Conservative Government. With tax policy friends like that, I would hate to be on the receiving end of the Government's enmity. The Government has hit, right between the eyes, middle class working men and women of Canada who try to keep the economy alive.
The Minister of Finance himself called sales tax the silent killer of jobs. Yet, since he has come to power along with his cohorts, individual Canadian families are paying an extra $500 a year, simply as a result of increased sales taxes and excise taxes on gas. That has to be coupled with $600, $700, or $800 extra in taxes as a result of the Government's so-called tax reform.
How can the Minister have any credibility? How can he try, with a straight face, to convince the people of Canada that it is the Opposition that is somehow preventing the work of Parliament from being done? Considering the complexity of the trade Bill, I daresay that we could use all the time between now and the beginning of July to detail our very specific opposition to it. It is such a bad Bill, that we are convinced the people of Canada will realize that once they have time to read the fine print.
Commercial blood banks are included in the free trade deal. The Minister from St. John's West sold out Newfoundlanders today. Obviously he does not care about selling out the national health care system. It is right in the annex of the trade deal that blood banks of a commercial nature will be allowed, and that will result in the destruction of the Canadian medicare system as we now know it.
I am not saying that next year we will have to pay for blood, but we will soon, if a private market captures 5 per cent to 10 per cent of the Canadian market for the sale of blood. If I set up an office in downtown Toronto and offer people fifty bucks for a pint of blood, how long do you think, Mr. Speaker, the voluntary sector of the Red Cross will be able to continue the well developed national network of voluntary blood clinics which has become a hallmark of this country?
Yes, we would like time to debate the substantive issues. The Deputy House Leader for the Government said that the Opposition was obstructing real debate. Since last week we have been wanting to have a real debate on this issue, and the Government itself has determined that it would rather be faced with the ringing of the bells on procedural matters. I am one of those who thinks the public wants to hear a debate of substance, and we would like to debate the substance.
In the space of two weeks I cannot represent the people of Hamilton East on the tax package alone. How can I be expected to stand silent while I watch this rip-off and the padding of the rich? According to the Government's own figures we know that even after this so-called tax reform more than 60,000 profitable corporations will still be paying no tax, even though the Government promised a minimum tax on the rich. We also know that 5,220 rich individuals will be paying no tax, even though the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised a minimum tax on the rich.
Yes, there are points we would like to raise on tax reform and literally dozens of other Bills on which would wish to have a chance to articulate.


How does the Government expect us to deal with the trade Bill, the abortion resolution, the tax reform legislation, the national parks legislation, the mutual legal assistance legislation, the proceeds of crime legislation, the official languages legislation, the Canada-Nova Scotia offshore petroleum resources legislation, the registration of lobbyists legislation, the Canadian Wheat Board legislation, the Canadian National Trade Tribunal legislation, the divestiture of Eldorado Nuclear Limited legislation, the Canada Labour Code legislation, the Bretton Woods Agreement legislation, the National Housing and CMHC Acts, the Canadian Grain Act, the conflict of interest Senate and House of Commons Act, the Department of Industry, Science and Technology Act, the Multiculturalism Act, the Immigration Refugee Act, the Immigration Refugee Illegal Act, Air Canada privatization, pari mutuel betting- the Government is moving into pari mutuel betting through a new Bill which has come forward-the National Transportation Act, and amendments for disabled persons?
That only includes the Government's list of demands for the next two weeks of legislation already on the Order Paper. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) promised that he was going to come forward with a child care Act, but we have not seen it yet. We have also been waiting to hear about a number of other Acts which have not yet come forward. The Government is demanding that they be passed before we even see them.
If we as Members are to take our responsibilities seriously, surely we owe it to the taxpayers who are going to be footing the bill for this monstrosity to examine every clause in a detailed way and to ensure that whatever legislation is passed is good legislation, or at least that the arguments on both sides will have been well aired.
The Government is not interested in real debate. It was already talking closure when we had had six speakers, I believe, and it had had six or seven speakers on one Bill. The Government is really interested in muzzling the Opposition and ramming through a rather poor quality of debate.
I heard government Members laughing during Question Period when the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell (Mr. Boudria) spoke about the work of the employees of the House of Commons. They laughed because most of them sit in their offices and do not have to do anything anyway. I have spoken to a number of employees of the House of Commons. Those sitting right in this room who work in translation are not even covered by the Canada Labour Code. They do not even have the basic conditions of their workplace guaranteed, which is the minimum basic right given to every other Canadian worker. When the Government introduced the legislation on unionization of employees on the Hill, unfortunately it forgot to proclaim the part which dealt with working conditions.
Translators work at a very high stress job. God forbid that the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDer-mid) should get his "blues" with the wrong phrase or he will
Extension of Sittings
be on his feet on another false point of order. These individuals work extremely hard and deserve support rather than the cackles and guffaws which we heard from Members of the Conservative Party who seem to think that no one else in Parliament knows the meaning of work. If the debate continues until ten, eleven, twelve, or one o'clock in the morning and the quality of it continues to decline, the employees have to continue to take the notes and translate the Debates.
I think they and the taxpayers of Canada are at least entitled to a quality of debate which is being denied by this legislation. This is in fact a false way for the 140 Conservative Members of Parliament who know they will not be back in the House of Commons after the next election to enjoy an extended vacation.
While my colleagues are here in the House to continue the debate and maintain quorum as we have done over the last four years, this is a make-holiday program for tired Tories who know that they have no hope and might as well live out their last days in their swimming pools.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I am sure that we will keep them here.
The question in my mind is: Why are we debating a motion to extend the sitting of this House until September 9? What is the justification for this? The Government says that it has run such a successful Parliament that 197 Bills received Royal Assent as well as some Private Members' Bills, perhaps 203 or 204 altogether. It boasts about how successful this Parliament has been. There was no question that the Opposition was


Extension of Sittings
blocking the work of Parliament. It was obviously a very hard working Parliament which passed so many Bills.
What is the justification for this? We know the justification. It is that the Government now wants to pass the free trade Bill, Bill C-130, and we have said: "They shall not pass". We have said that quite clearly, because the people of Canada have not had an opportunity to participate in the discussion about the free trade agreement. Was it raised in 1984? Not on your bippy, Mr. Speaker, it was not raised at all.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was running for Leader of the Conservative Party in 1983-and I do not know why anyone would want to run for the leadership of that Party-he said: "free trade with the United States is like getting into bed with an elephant. If the elephant rolls over you are dead". That is all he was on record as saying with regard to free trade. It is clear and unequivocal opposition to free trade.
Now that he is the Prime Minister we are being told that we have to sit through the summer so that he can ram Bill C-130 through Parliament. We all know now why he cannot be trusted. He speaks out of both sides of his mouth. Someone said that one can always tell when the Prime Minister is not being straight with the folks, because he moves his lips.
The Prime Minister is trying to put free trade through the House of Commons at the last moment before it breaks on June 30. The Government is extending the sitting of the House so he can ram through Bill C-130. We are saying that that is not fair to the people of Canada. Canadians have a right to participate in a deal which will be so important to the future of our country.
We have challenged the Prime Minister to call an election and make this an issue, but he will not touch it. Here we have this phalanx of Tories gathered here to try to extend the sitting. We have opposed it.
The Government has even brought in closure in order to get the motion through. It is the tyranny of the majority on 70 members in the Opposition. Those 200-odd Members on the government side should be ashamed of themselves for picking on so small an opposition. One would think that their conscience would at least bother them, but Tories do not have consciences.
This is what the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) had to say about closure in 1981, with regard to the Excise Tax Act introduced by the Liberal Government. As reported at page 10409 of Hansard on June 9, 1981, the Hon. Member for St. John's West, the present Minister for International Trade, said:
This comes from a closure-crazed government, a government which suffers from the crime of parliamentary bestiality. It cannot wait to force these kinds of things through the House.
He went on to say:
The same little group comes in here on every closure motion. The same little group of parliamentary eunuchs, the same group of parliamentary assassins- the House leader, the assistant House leader, the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres)-are in here all the time, assassinating this House and removing the good from the House. That is why I call them the parliamentary eunuchs. The good has already been removed from them.
Then he says:
This is an illustration of what has happened to Canada. Today we have a parliamentary system of government without any checks and balances and without the separation of powers. The Prime Minister has a group of docile sheep in his caucus who keep him in power, no matter what he is doing. They just say "Baaa, sir, baaa, sir, pass it through the House, sir". As long as they do that, he has absolute power. This Prime Minister has absolute power as long as the majority in his caucus give him that unlimited power. They are so busy with their noses in the patronage trough and the power trough that they neither know nor care what happens to this Parliament, and we can expect nothing from them.
Can you believe that, Mr. Speaker? That was stated by one of the power brokers in the Tory caucus when he was in opposition. Now he is in government and the eunuchs have moved over from the Opposition. Look at all the eunuchs on the back-benches. "Baa, baa".
The Prime Minister had to go to Paris to get the ambassador to run in Lac-Saint-Jean to save the Government's skin in Quebec. What message is he giving to the eunuchs in the backbenches who have been elected from that part of the country? He is telling them that they are a bunch of eunuchs who he cannot trust to save his skin. He went to Paris for Lucien Bouchard.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: He is going to win tonight and you are going to finish third.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
You fellows will never make it to Cabinet. You were overlooked. I suppose they are fulfilling the function for which they were elected, which is to flip their flippers like trained seals.
The Government is only extending the sitting of this Parliament in order to pass its trade deal. It is not interested in what Canadians think. Otherwise it would provide an appropriate time to debate the Bill properly throughout the land. The parliamentary committee should be travelling throughout the country to receive briefs from Canadians, to listen to their concerns, and to inform them.
The Government has put millions of dollars in the trough while the Minister for International Trade hires his best friend to spread the propaganda to Canadians before the Bill has even passed second reading. The Government is only interested in the propaganda. It is following all the same practices which brought down the Liberal Government and for which the Conservatives condemned the previous Liberal Government. It has introduced time allocation numerous times in this Parliament and has brought in closure many times in the exact same fashion as have the Liberals. The Conservatives promised a new era but they have not done anything different.



The Conservatives promised that there would be no more patronage. Canadians still remember when the Prime Minister said to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner): "You had an option, sir". Lo and behold, the patronage machines are still operating.
The Prime Minister said that it was reprehensible to buy Canadian voters with their own money.
Yet we have the spectacle of the Prime Minister on a sojourn to Lac-Saint-Jean trying to buy the by-election for his friend. It seems the only people who can get anywhere in this country are classmates or room-mates of the Prime Minister. The treasury doors have been opened. Where is restraint? Out the window. We do not hear too much talk now about the deficit. The Conservatives are on a spending splurge, trying to buy a friend a seat in the House of Commons, all because the Prime Minister could not trust Members of Parliament who were elected under the Tory banner from the Province of Quebec.
What he is really saying to them is: "You can't be trusted". What the Prime Minister is attempting to do is to buy the voters of Lac-Saint-Jean with their own money. I do not think the people of Lac-Saint-Jean are going to fall for that. The Conservatives tried to buy St. John's East and that did not work. But did the people of St. John's East get the $30 million? They sure did. So the people of Lac-Saint-Jean could boot Lucien Bouchard out and still get the money because the other Bouchard has to come across because he is in a nearby riding. How can the Conservatives turn off the tap? They promised it, and if the people do not vote for their candidate, they still have to be given the money.
Today we heard about the Newfoundland railway. It is gone. They are going to replace it with highways. Just imagine, we can have a new highway built all the way from Alma to Labrador, and then we can put a causeway over to Newfoundland and we can make it the Trans-Canada. That is the spectacle. We have to extend this sitting because the Government wants to pass Bill C-130, which will put the free trade arrangement between the Prime Minister of this country and Ronald Reagan into effect. It is a giveaway of this country to the United States. It is a sell-out.
Canadians have many questions. First, they are not aware of all the details of this agreement and what they have been hearing, they do not like. They do not believe, for example, that a foreign government ought to dictate to a Canadian Government, which was elected by the people, as to how our energy should be priced. That ought not to be a prerogative of any foreign government. Second, what Canadians do not like is the virtual elimination of all review of American investments in this country. At a time when the Americans are becoming very concerned about Asian investment in the United States, the Canadian Government is turning over the country to the
Extension of Sittings
United States. I think Canadians are very concerned that we will become the fifty-first State.
This deal should not be proceeded with until the Canadian people have been consulted. There are enough Bills on the Order Paper that our caucus is prepared to support. For example, we said we were prepared to support the lobbying Bill. The Prime Minister committed himself to that two years ago on an urgent basis. He said: "We will bring in a lobbying Bill, a Bill to register lobbyists", because he was concerned. He wanted to establish a Mr. Clean image and his friends, Doucette and Ouellet the card-player, all of them wanted to create a clean image, so he promised the Lobbying Registry, Bill C-82. It is called the Frank Moores Bill. We are all set to pass Bill C-82. So why does the Government not bring forward the Frank Moores Bill? We are ready for it.
We had a report on bank service charges. The Government has promised us a Bill. Bring it on and if it is patterned along the lines of our report, we will pass it. The Government does not have to extend the House in order for us to pass it. We will pass it because we recognize that there are some Bills on the Order Paper about which we agree. We can pass those Bills.
I just mentioned Bill C-82. We are prepared to pass that. We passed Bill C-31, the Railway Act, on Friday. We passed it through all stages. We can do that with Bill C-82 and with the amendment to the Bank Act, along the lines of the committee report. After all, we even drafted the report and entered it as a Private Member's Bill. All the Government has to do is present it. We will pass it. In fact, if the Government does not want to do that, it can go the private Member's route and we will pass it that way. But the Government will not do that because the banks are its friends. They are the government's bankers. I see the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), here. He is very useful to have in the Tory caucus because he can walk both sides of the street. He is the enemy of the banks but he is a Tory at the same time. It is a nice game, but it will not wash.

speechtext:
I suspect that before there are too many moons through the sky, a Bill of that nature might be before us. However, the issue today is in connection with what amounts to unrealistic delays in the basic program of the


Extension of Sittings
Government. Every time we have tried to move ahead with that basic program, the coalition represented by the Liberal New Dinosaur Party has done everything it can to make sure that this House is hijacked to the effect that the thrust of the government's move on privatization, the thrust of the government's move with respect to a trade agreement, the thrust of the government's move with respect to cleaning up the problem of illegal immigration and the thrust of the government's work on a free vote on abortion, has been stymied, held up and delayed unrealistically. The Opposition knows that. It has made a point of declaring that it would use every conceivable delaying method possible to prevent debate, discussion, committee meetings, that it would do everything to force those Bills and those government initiatives to be stopped.
Clearly, a Government which intends to run the country has to ensure that Parliament works and that it has a chance to debate the issues before it, particularly the issues brought to the attention of Parliament by the Government. I do not think we had one sensible debate all last week. We had one motion after another as to whether a private Member should be entitled to introduce a Bill and one vote after another as to whether that Bill should be printed and circulated. That is an unrealistic waste of time for which the taxpayers paid in hiring us to be their representatives in this House of Commons. There is no justification for it. That time has to be made up. Unfortunately, that time is going to have to be made up in July. None of us like that. None of us want that. That make-up of time is totally unnecessary.
In other Parliaments in this Commonwealth serious matters that are in complete debate between one side or the other, where both sides have their own firm position, are handled in one day, perhaps a day and a half with perhaps two speakers from each side, perhaps not even that, and a vote is called. That is what happens in Great Britain. Here we have one filibuster after another, one delaying tactic after another. There may be a point in that, but the point is that we have to sit longer than we should have to sit, because we do have to come to grips with the issues. We do not solve the problem of Parliament by delaying techniques that prevent us from coming to grips with issues. We are paid to come to grips with issues. We are paid to make decisions. We are paid to show leadership. We are not paid to vote on whether or not a Member should be able to introduce a Bill.
The coalition has brought us to this. We have been forced by the coalition to extend the hours of the House, to extend the sittings of the House in order that the Government-needed legislation can be dealt with. The coalition says: "Call an election". There are signs out that state: "Trade Mulroney and call an election". Sir, they will have an election. But they want an election before the fourteenth of July, because they want to have a Parliament elected improperly. They want a Parliament that is not representative of the people. They want to force on
Canada a Parliament based on a 1971 census. That is the extent of their idea of democracy.
This coalition has nothing to offer Canada other than delay, other than harping criticism. They have no program, no philosophy other than socialism, state ownership, as the means of production and distribution. This is a coalition of those who believe in big government. This is a coalition of those who believe in big brother. They will have an opportunity to present their ideas of big brother, probably before the snow flies, but not before we have redistribution. They know that, and this hollow call for an election is exactly that, a hollow call from hollow minds. The issues in the election, Sir, will be the trade issue, whether Canada is going to offer opportunities for young people, or whether those opportunities will only be available in the United States.
We are a nation of 25 million people. There is presently a meeting of the G-7 in Toronto. Our trading partners all have markets in excess of 100 billion people at home. We have a market of 25 million. How do we ever expect to be world competitive without at least a basic home market? Yet, the coalition says: "Don't worry about that. Put a big fence around Canada and make sure we have a little Canada." We will have an opportunity to discuss that with the people of Canada. The people of Canada will vote for a big Canada, a future for their kids. That is the type of Canada we want, and that is the type of Canada that the people will have a chance to vote for. But, they will get a chance after redistribution, not before. They will get a chance after the trade Bill is passed at least the House of Commons.
In this Bill we will be able to show exactly what we intend to do, and we will be able to have the people vote on this Bill and the trade issues. The coalition will have to say that they do not want to deal with the United States. One of them is going to tear it up, the other is going to tear it down. I do not know how the tearing is going. But I can tell you, Sir, the tearing is going to be the tearing of the Liberal-New Democratic coalition, the tweedle-dum and the tweedle-dee of the House.
The Government has a program of privatization. We have been moving the Government out of the affairs of individuals. In the last three and a half years we have privatized more Crown corporations than all of the Governments put together, both federal and provincial, in the history of Canada. Before the House we have a major privatization Bill involving Air Canada. That Bill is demanded by over 80 per cent of the employees of Air Canada. It will enable our national airline to compete in the world without having its hands tied behind its back as an agent of the Crown. It is important to the people of Canada that that Bill goes through. We can have a vote on it and the coalition can renationalize it, if they want to, if the people of Canada direct them that way. But the airline employees will not vote for them when they have an opportunity to buy stock in their company.
I come now to the immigration matter. This House was called back in emergency session on August 10, 1987. It was


recalled to deal with the flagrant abuses of our immigration laws whereby people would come across our border and say: "I am a refugee", because they knew that under the present system, a system formulated by the Liberal Party, they could stay in Canada for five years and work anyway, because they could go from one appeal and one delaying process to another. As a result, our immigration system is now clogged with more than 50,000 people claiming refugee status, most of them improperly.
It is not that they do not want to come to Canada, and not that most of them might make good immigrants, but they are trying to jump the queue. We have Bills that have been delayed in the Senate for more than 200 days that would deal with that problem. The issue in the election will be the Senate, directed by Allan MacEachen, which believes that it does not need to be elected in order to stymie the will of the elected people and be responsive to the electorate. They will get their election all right, and the election will be on the Senate that has done its darndest to hamper and prevent democracy from working, since 1984 only.
Sir, we have to have an extension of hours. I do not like to have an extension of hours. It is unfortunate. But when there is continual blocking of the activity of the Elouse by a coalition on the other side, determined to prevent matters from coming to a vote, determined to prevent open and free debate, and determined to make sure that an agenda reasonably put to it by the House Leaders is negotiated and worked out, then the Government has no choice except to move to set aside the rules on a temporary basis to give that opportunity demanded for debate.
They do not want debate. They only want to play blunder-log, a game we used to play with cub scouts. They want to destroy things. They do not want to build a Canada. They do not want to get at the problems of Canada.
We have an abortion resolution on which they state: "Don't give us a free vote on it." That would be undemocratic to vote freely! That is a mark of the Liberal-New Democratic Party coalition: no freedom. In the New Democratic Party they say: "There can be no free vote. We will control our Members. They will march to one drum only". On issues of moral conscience we always believe that the will of the Members ought to prevail. Surely, on this matter or any matter it ought to be brought forward for an open discussion in this House in a realistic time frame and a vote should be taken, a vote which would give every Member of Parliament the opportunity to take one or the other propositions put to him or to her.
The point of the whole matter is that we need to have the opportunity as a Government to govern. We cannot have that opportunity to govern stymied by misuse and abuse of the rules. What we have had to do today is to move a closure motion to temporarily change the rules, something which will

enable us to come to grips with the problems that affect this country.

My friend says that we should be ashamed of ourselves. He is saying, as Liberals or New Democrats say, that we should be ashamed of ourselves for governing the country. Sir, I say that we have an obligation to govern the country. We have demonstrated our ability and our will to do that. My friend has demonstrated absolutely no policy, no thrust or no leadership.
Members opposite will have an opportunity in the debates in the weeks ahead if they want to continue to talk. But this motion gives them a lot of opportunity to talk. Let us hear what they have to say. If they are sensible, let us get the matters that are before the House dealt with so that we can get on to more important issues, and perhaps an election.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 26 in the name of the Government is a motion which seeks to set aside a certain number of our Standing Orders so that the House may sit as late as September 9, and with extended hours. This motion has been justified by the Government on several grounds. These Government arguments for Motion No. 26 may be quickly summarized as follows.
First, we need Motion No. 26, these extra days and these extended hours, because there has been considerable Opposition obstruction; and this obstruction has come in this Parliament not only from the two Opposition Parties but it has come as well from the Senate.
The second argument is that extra days and hours are needed in order to clear the Order Paper.
Third, the Government says that it has had foisted upon it some unanticipated measures. It refers to the ghost of Meech Lake which has returned from the Senate, let us call it Meech Lake II, which has now been partly demystified and shown, I think, by the other place to be a bad piece of constitutional amending. Second, the Supreme Court of Canada has struck down the abortion law and made it necessary for this Parliament to decide what must be done with this political, this social, this moral issue.
Fourth, it is said that we must sit through the summer and late into each night because it is in the public interest so to do.
Finally, the Minister of State said that Parliament must deal with the free trade question.
I intend to look at those arguments and test their validity to the best of my ability. First, I will deal with obstruction.
I would like to ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether this Parliament has really been characterized by excessive, by unusual, by unwarranted obstruction tactics by the two Opposition Parties. We know for a fact that the Government has vigorously used time allocation and closure, plus a variety of new


Extension of Sittings
methods not frequently used in the past which have allowed it to push ahead with its plans and its schedule.
In 44 months of this Parliament, 204 Bills have been passed.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
The Minister of State bragged about that accomplishment. He pointed out to Hon. Members that in the Parliament of 1974-79 and in the Parliament of 1980-84 only 177 Bills were passed in each case, and those two Parliaments sat longer than has the current Parliament.
I want to ask this question. Where is the Government's case for obstruction? It cannot be proven because there has been no obstruction, unless the Government argues that the legitimate role of the Opposition is in itself obstruction.
Perhaps the huge majority that it acquired in 1984 has whetted its appetite to have a one-party state. I want to say that if that is the case it is not going to happen by any decision made in this Parliament. It will only happen when the Canadian people decide that every constituency should be represented by a Progressive Conservative and not by the representative of any other Party. You know and I know, Mr. Speaker, that that is highly unlikely to happen. It is far more likely that this Government will be ejected from office.
The Minister of State also referred to his problems with the Senate. He says that the Senate has used its constitutional powers in this Parliament, and quite legitimate powers, I would say. They have been used, and I would say, generally speaking, they have been used effectively and responsibly. I am now absolutely convinced that in a federal state we need a bicameral system. We need two Chambers in order to check more effectively a powerful administration, an excessively strong executive branch of government which exists in the Canadian system. If two Opposition Parties cannot do it, then we may have to alter our system so that it can be done regularly and systematically. We have to check power because we have seen in this Parliament the abuse of power.
However, the second House, the Senate, I believe must have legitimacy. I believe that can only be acquired by means of election.
I have no sympathy with the Government when it claims that it is having problems with the Senate. It has had four years up until now to do something about it. It could have reformed the Senate. Yet all it did at Meech Lake was to transfer appointments from the Prime Minister to the Premiers, thereby guaranteeing that we are highly unlikely ever to see an elected Senate in this country.
When the Canadian politburo met at Meech Lake to declare Quebec a constitutionally distinct society, why did it not at the same time move to abolish an appointed Senate and put into place mechanisms that would be required for an elected Senate? We all agree that an appointed Senate is an anathema to democracy. But why has the Government not moved to change it? It did not do so because it knows that it would be
cutting off its own nose to spite its face. It, too, uses the Senate for its own partisan purposes. Given this situation, any ranting and raving from particular Ministers or the Government collectively about the Senate make no impression at all on this Hon. Member. Thus we can set aside the obstructionist argument. There has not been any from either the House of Commons or the Senate.
The second proposition from the Government is that we need Motion No. 26 in order to clear the Order Paper. The Minister of State has written to the Opposition House Leaders with a list of what he considers on the Order Paper that it is necessary to dispose of in this session of Parliament. Sir, there are 41 Bills and/or motions that he has put forward. It is an imposing list. But it seems to me when I looked at that list that there is plenty of room there, as the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) said, for some negotiation, for some bargaining, for some compromise, in order to achieve a workable schedule.
The only requirement in order to do that, Sir, would be to have some skill, some openness, some flexibility, some common sense and some reason displayed by the three Government House Leaders.
On top of this we have had these two unanticipated issues, Meech Lake II and the abortion question. The first of these will be disposed of Wednesday of this week when the House will divide on the Meech Lake motion. That leaves abortion, Mr. Speaker. We could have been using these June evenings to debate the abortion question. It would have been helpful to all Hon. Members if we had known what the Government's position was. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) promised he would give leadership.
This Government has a position on absolutely everything. That position that it takes is ironclad. It says: " We have to get the motion through. We will use our majority to get it through". The Government has a position on everything except when it comes to a delicate and sensitive issue like abortion. Suddenly, isn't it amazing how democratic and open the Government gets? Why isn't the Government like that on a lot more issues?
That leaves two of the Government's arguments yet to be considered, those that I outlined at the beginning. Let me deal with the public interest. The Government says it is in the public interest to keep the House in session all summer, sitting each day, late into the evening. I would say to you, Sir, that no elected Member of this House can ever play down or argue against the public interest proposition. We are here in the public interest. The public interest is paramount. It takes precedence over partisan interest. It takes precedence over personal interest. We are here in the public interest. The question is how do you judge which particular item or group of items are absolutely in the public interest? How do you decide

When negotiations break down, when common sense and good reason does not work, then we can only do what is left open to us and that is to seek arbitration, first through the Speaker, and then, on the very big items, we have to go to the people of the country to get their opinion on whether they want to proceed with matters so vital as free trade with the United States of America and a Meech Lake Accord which is changing the basic law of this country.

speechtext:
That is good for Canadians to see and hear as well. That kind of behaviour is helpful to the Government.
1 decided to enter this debate because of comments made a little earlier by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps). Those of us who were sitting in the House will recall that she said something to the effect that there had been no contribution made by the Hamilton-area Members of Parliament. She went so far as to say that there were Hamilton-area Members who had not said anything of substance on some of the major issues. When I hear nonsense like that, it behoves me and everyone who is present in the House on a day-to-day basis and is involved with committee work and constituency work to challenge statements like the one made by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East.
As the Hon. Member was saying that, 1 had to think of my four colleagues from the Hamilton area and of some of the contributions 1 know they have made. You are well acquainted with the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling), Mr. Speaker. I do not have to remind you of the contributions of the Hon. Member for Burlington as chief government Whip in
the Cabinet in which you served in the Thirty-first Parliament. He is presently the Chairman of the private Members' committee.
The whole idea of parliamentary reform may be out of fashion. We have seen on a day-to-day basis the actions of the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party and how they are trying to thwart parliamentary reform, but Members like the Hon. Member for Burlington, who is the chairman of the private Members' committee, are spearheading reform and are true to the spirit of reform for private Members. That Hon. Member should be congratulated on that account by all Members of Parliament.
I thought as well of my good friend and colleague, a good friend of this House and, I would suggest, a good friend of Canadians, the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Peterson). We are aware that he is Vice-Chairman of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs. We know of his contributions on that committee and of his contributions in the House. One of the things that has always struck me about him, and I met him just shortly after being elected, is that he is one of those individuals who works day and night on behalf of his constituents in the Hamilton area. Not a day goes by that he is not involved in some way in trying to solve problems. I ask the Hon. Member for Hamilton East and other members of the New Democratic and Liberal Parties, is that not the kind of Member that Canada wants? Is that not the kind of Member that Canada should have in the House of Commons? I know that the people of his riding are very pleased and honoured to have the Hon. Member for Hamilton West represent them in this House.
I thought as well of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott). I am aware, of course, that he is Chairman of the Standing Committee on Secretary of State. I know how involved he is in the day-to-day operations of this House and of his many valuable interventions on behalf of all Canadians and particularly on behalf of the people of Hamilton-Wentworth. As someone who does not come from the Hamilton area, I think of all he has done and said on behalf of the Hamilton airport in order to improve service there. I am sure that the people of the Hamilton area and indeed the people of the Niagara area from which I come appreciate the very valuable service he has done for that area and for many other areas over the past 10 years.
Finally, I come to the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mrs. Martin). I would guess that I know her the best of those four Members of Parliament, having served with her on the special committee on child care. I know as well that she is the Chairman of the National Progressive Conservative Party and I know of the valuable work she does there.
I do know as well that long after the Hon. Member for Hamilton East is but a footnote in the Thirty-third Parliament, the contributions of the Hon. Member for Lincoln in the area of child care will not be forgotten. The report of the committee


of which she was chairman is something that will be of lasting contribution to the well-being of Canadian children and something that will live on far beyond the life of this Parliament.
What Canada needs is more people like the Hon. Member for Lincoln and more people like the Conservative Members from Hamilton. If we had more Members from the Hamilton area as effective as the four Progressive Conservative Members, it would be better for the Hamilton area and certainly better for Canada.
The Hon. Member for Hamilton East says that the Progressive Conservative Members from the Hamilton area do not speak enough. I just wonder if it has ever occurred to her even once that perhaps she speaks too much, that she speaks too much for the good that she does.
Members of the Opposition are saying that we should call the election right now, dissolve the House. That is their solution to the problems that face Canada. The Hon. Member from Mississauga made a very good point. If we called an election now, redistribution would not be in effect. There are presently two Members of Parliament from the Mississauga area. In the Brampton area, and in Mississauga as well, there are as many as four times the national population average for one riding. It is easy to say that the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) and the two Members from Mississauga are four times as effective as Members from the New Democratic Party or the Liberal Party, but I do not think that is an answer. I do not think it is fair to the people from those areas to have the opposition Parties call for an immediate dissolution of Parliament.
I think of the abortion question as well. For a number of my colleagues, this is a very important issue. There is no abortion law on the books of Canada right now. That means that unborn children are being killed because there is no protection for them. On whose conscience would it be if this Parliament fails to act on that?
I am aware that the very reasonable approach of the Government, one that was alluded to in the editorial in today's Globe and Mail, is being fought in the name of democracy by the members of the New Democratic and Liberal Parties. I think it is a shame that they are opposing bringing forward that resolution that can and will do so much to protect unborn children.
I think as well of the refugee Bills. We would be much further ahead if we did not have this stalling. Who is to blame for the fact that Canada does not have a rational, working refugee determination system? It is the Members of the Liberal Party, the Party of the Member for Hamilton East How many thousands of people have come into this country and abused the system because Bills C-55 and C-84 have not long since been passed?

With regard to the complaints of the Liberal Party, they should tell their colleagues in the Senate that they should be sitting every day, they should be spending 24 hours a day down the hall in order to get this legislation through Parliament because that is what Canadians are demanding.

speechtext:
I am informed that they do not sit Mondays. They should be sitting Mondays, Saturdays, and around the clock to clean up the backlog of legislation which has been sent to them by this House.
Members of the Opposition do not want to be here and it is good for Canadians to hear that. Members of the Opposition want to be in their ridings across the country. The nonsense that you hear on a day-to-day basis in the House of Commons, Mr. Speaker, is only equalled by the nonsense, misinformation, and fear they are spreading across the country.
My own riding of Niagara Falls is no exception. Recently the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) was in town. I do not know how often he has been to the Niagara Peninsula. He is like some of those self-proclaimed experts on the Niagara Peninsula. They blow in for a cup of coffee, stay for an hour, and say: "I'm an expert on the Niagara Peninsula, I'll tell you that free trade is no good for the area". Every time they open their mouths in that way they show just how little they know about the Niagara Peninsula.
They make comments about the grape and wine industry. I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) in the House. He is going to bring forward a proposal which will assist that industry. It will be one of the most constructive things that has happened to that industry in years.
The Leader of the Opposition and other Members come to the Niagara Peninsula and say that the free trade agreement is no good, it should be torn up, it is bad for the Niagara area. That is nonsense. They only say that because they never talk to anyone on the Niagara Peninsula. They pretend that the Niagara Peninsula is a one-industry area and base their comments on that single industry.
That is absolutely wrong. The Niagara Peninsula is as diverse as is any other area in Canada. If they spent two hours on the Niagara Peninsula instead of one they could drop by the Ford Motor Corporation. The Ford Motor Corporation has approached me and told me that as their representative I must support the free trade agreement because everything they make in Niagara Falls is shipped across the border into the United States. That is why they need open access to the borders and that is why they support the free trade agreement.
The general manager of General Motors has sent a letter to every single employee of General Motors Canada saying that this agreement is good for General Motors, good for the auto industry, good for Oshawa, good for St. Catharines, and good for Canada. Members of the Liberal and New Democratic Parties never refer to that. They forget about that.


Public Service Employment Act
If they spent a little more time in my area they might drop by the TRW plant. I was there and at the Hayes Dana plant. I asked the managers and people who work there whether they can compete in an open market. They said that they will not only compete but will do very well. They do not compete only on a North American basis. The auto parts made on the Niagara Peninsula are world competitive. They tell me that my job is to ensure that the border remains open and they will do very well. That is never referred to by the NDP or the Liberals.
They never stopped in at Brunner Manufacturing, another company with huge exports to the United States. I was at Edsha Corporation two weeks ago. That company is only one year old and at that moment was hiring its one hundred and forty-first and one hundred and forty second employee in the auto parts industry. Their message to me was the same, keep the border open. They are there in order to export into the United States.
Members of the New Democratic Party and Members of the Liberal Party are interested only in spreading fear and misinformation in the Niagara Peninsula. I will not stand by while misinformation and fear is spread by socialists and Members of the Liberal Party. I will not stand by while those who do not know a thing about the Niagara Peninsula blow in and proclaim themselves experts. I will fight that, here in the House of Commons, in my riding, and across Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, wish to enter into this debate. I would like to explain to the Canadian people watching the proceedings of the House on television this afternoon what this debate is really all about. The Government has requested, through a motion, to extend the sitting hours of Parliament in order that Parliament can deal with pieces of legislation which the Government insists it needs.
One of the chief pieces of legislation is the legislation which would put into law the agreement signed between the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of this country, the Reagan-Mulroney trade deal. The Opposition, both the Liberal and New Democratic Parties, are quite opposed to this piece of legislation, mainly because we believe that the Government has no mandate to proceed with this.
We believe that by extending the hours of Parliament and the number of days that Parliament will sit in the summer, the Government has torn up the rule books by which Parliament governs itself. As opposition Members it is our duty, in the parliamentary system, to try to prevent the Government from proceeding with its plans. We have heard government Members state that the Government needs this legislation to extend the sitting hours because the Government was elected to govern and needs this extended sitting in order to do so.
There is so much in Canadian parliamentary democracy which depends upon consensus. It is true that there are fundamental differences between political Parties in terms of
our outlook on how the country should be governed. However, there is also a general agreement-and that is why Parliament can work-that the Government should be able to govern, that the Opposition does have a role, and that Parliament should be able to function.
Very often this consensus is unstated. We will rise in our place in Parliament and object to particular pieces of legislation, but at some stage we recognize that it is the Government's right to proceed with its legislation and allow the vote to occur. Thus, legislation becomes law.
