speechtext:
Absolutely. The French equivalent of vacation is vacance, and that is the word for recess. The Hon. Member knows that. If the Hon. Member cannot face reality, that is his problem.
Several Hon. Members have said that this motion should be opposed and defeated because Members need vacations. They need to get away. They have said they need to get away for family reasons as well as for constituency reasons. They need to get away for personal reasons. One Hon. Member of the NDP said that he had his own personal agenda and that this motion was interfering with it. That is the kind of reasoning that has been put before the House in opposition to this motion.
Of course, we do need vacations. We need opportunities to go home, and the Hon. Member who just spoke has certainly been home to speak to his constituents. I believe he just won a hotly contested nomination battle, and that is to his credit. He certainly had to go home and speak to his constituents to do that, and he had time to do so.
This motion, along with the rest of the business of the House, is not preventing Members from getting home to speak to their constituents and to do their work. This motion requires that the House stay in session to deal with the business of the Government and the business of the House. Surely that is our priority, and it must be our priority.
We were called back last August to deal with an emergency occasioned by false refugees. This House dealt with it. The Senate tried to thwart the will of the House, even as the Opposition tried to delay it by filibuster. We dealt with this Bill today in its final form because of those delaying tactics, not because of the lack of will on the part of the Government or lack of dedication on the part of Members of the House.
A second reason has been raised, namely, that instead of extending the sitting of the House this summer the Government should call an election.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
I am shocked that a member of the Liberal Party would applaud that when he knows that it would rob certain communities of this country of the right to the representation they need through redistribution. After the middle of July the City of Scarborough will be entitled to five seats. I take it that the Liberal Party wants to deny the City of Scarborough that. They want to deny other parts of the country the enlarged representation which redistribution will give them.
Extension of Sittings
A lot of us recognize that there is merit in extending the life of this Parliament until redistribution can take effect. The Province of Ontario can have more seats, the Province of Alberta can have more seats, the Province of British Columbia can have more seats, and people can have the representation that their population justifies.
The real reason the Opposition wants to have an election before we can pass the legislation that is the purpose of these extended sittings is that they want to deny the Government the record of achievement which will be represented by passing the legislation and resolutions which will be part of this summer's work. Oppositions know that Governments get credit only for what is passed by the House. Oppositions benefit from delaying it beyond any possibility of being passed.
I have to believe that the Opposition does not want the forthcoming election to be fought on the Government's record. Instead, they want it to be fought on what has been the basis of so many Question Periods, that is, sleaze, scandal-monger-ing, and character assassinations. By sitting into the summer we will have the opportunity to deal with the major issues which will be before us which need finalization by this House.
Finally, I want to respond to a point which has been made by the Opposition over and over again, that is, that Order No. 26 represents tyranny by the majority. It is a curious definition of democracy that the majority making a decision is somehow tyranny and that, by implication, the minority should have the right either to make the decision or to see that no decision will be made.
I can quote one outstanding authority on this. I wish there were some Liberals here to hear this. I can remember the former Liberal Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, objecting that after a reasonable period of debate there should be an opportunity for the House to make a decision, there should be an opportunity for a vote to be taken.
The reason we have the log-jam with which we are faced now, which requires us not to recess next week but to continue into the summer, is that the majority has been prevented from making the final decision which the majority should be able to make a decision on free trade, a decision on tax reform, a decision on Meech Lake, a decision on Air Canada, and decisions on other issues before us.
It is right that members of the Opposition should have time in which to make criticisms and constructive suggestions. It is right that they should have time to debate the issues in order that public opinion be informed and aroused. However, surely we do not need any imagination to realize that we have had more than sufficient time for the opposition Parties to do precisely that. Everyone knows that the Liberals and NDP Members are against free trade. They really do not need to hold this matter up any further. Everyone has heard the arguments for and against it and it is now time for this House to make a decision on that issue and others which are before us.


Extension of Sittings
In Order No. 26 we are not seeing tyranny by the majority but, in the resistance to it, we are seeing the threatened tyranny of the minority. It will be within the tradition of the Parliament of this land and others if the House is allowed, in the very near future, to make a decision by each of us doing what is our right and our duty, that is, to vote on these issues which have been so long before us and so long debated without each of us having the right to stand up and say yea or nay.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I always listen with interest to the Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) because even though I sometimes do not agree with him, he has a reputation for coherence, something which was absent tonight. In fact, I have never heard him so desperate. One could only be amused by someone who cites opposition obstruction to Meech Lake as one of the problems the Government was having when we know full well-

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext: I didn't do that.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
He did, he cited Meech Lake. We know that there has been all-Party agreement. There has been some dissent within caucuses, but basically Meech Lake has proceeded through this House with indecent haste. People have criticized Parliament in general for the lack of attention it has received. I point that out only to show how desperate the Hon. Member is for an argument tonight.
I want to speak a bit about what is happening in context of the parliamentary reforms which have taken place since 1982. After the bell-ringing crisis, a special committee of the House was struck chaired by the former Member of this House, Tom Lefebvre. I had an opportunity to serve on that committee and subsequently in this Parliament on a special committee on the reform of the House of Commons chaired by the former Member for St. John's East, Jim McGrath, who is now the Lieutenant-Governor of Newfoundland.
I want to put before you this evening, Mr. Speaker, my analysis of why what has happened here in the last week or so has been so damaging to both the spirit and the substance of those reforms. A lot of it is centred around the issue of the parliamentary calendar. There have been attempts made to trivialize opposition concern about the breaking of the parliamentary calendar by suggesting that people are only interested in their personal vacations, or whatever the case may be.
However, there is a much larger issue here, that is, whether, by virtue of the action taken by the Government last August when we were recalled to deal with what has obviously turned out not to be an emergency, and now being pushed beyond the end of June, again not as a result of any self-evident emergency but rather a perceived emergency in terms of the Government's own agenda, we will ever be able to return to the point where we have a parliamentary calendar. There are those who think that that was a good idea, not because of vacations but because it gave some form to the parliamentary year. I think
there is a legitimate concern to be expressed here, and not only in terms of losing the notion of a parliamentary calendar.
I might remind Hon. Members, and particularly the Government, that when the special committee selected this calendar, it included in it one more week of parliamentary business than the average number of weeks per year of parliamentary business over the 10 years preceding the recommendation of the committee. The time that the Government has had available to it under this calendar, in addition to the time which it created for itself by bringing us back in August, is far greater than was the average in the 10 years preceding the recommendation of the committee. My point is that it is not as though the Government has had only a small or limited amount of time. The special committee on the reform of the House of Commons erred, if you like, on the side of lengthier sittings.
The other point I want to make with respect to the parliamentary calendar is that it was part of a package. As I look back on those reforms and ask myself whether our expectations were ill-founded, I can say a number of things. I believe the reforms directed to private Members have worked reasonably well. There have been more free votes on Private Members' Bills the outcome of which we do not know. That is something the reform committee set out to create, and I believe it has been a success.
Perhaps the greatest example of its success, regardless of where one stands on the issue, was Bill C-204, the antismoking Bill.
The parliamentary calendar was part of a package of reforms which was agreed to in good faith and pursuant to which the Opposition gave up certain tactics at its disposal to delay business of the House. These included shorter speeches, and a requirement to have 15 Members present in order to prevent the extension of hours, a procedure which has been used increasingly as an indirect form of closure by the Government, which was not its intent. The Opposition gave up the power to ring the bells at great length, as the Conservative Opposition did in 1982. The Opposition forfeited a number of other procedures as part of that whole package in return for the notion of a parliamentary calendar.
In lieu of these concessions by the Opposition was the notion that there would be a set calendar regardless of whether the Government with its majority was able to pass legislation by a certain time of the year. There is nothing illegitimate about that. Those were the rules of the game.
We now have the parliamentary equivalent of the Government moving the goal posts. There was a consensual arrangement between the Parties for a package of reforms in which the Opposition and the Government made certain concessions. Only the Government has the power to take back unilaterally what it gave up in those negotiations. The Opposition does not have the power to take back what it gave up.


This motion is wrong because the Government is taking back elements of the package that was arrived at subsequent to 1982. If the Government is unable to pass legislation on its agenda by the June 30 deadline, there is a provision in the Standing Orders whereby it could appeal to the Speaker and make a case that there is an emergency. The Standing Orders as a result of the package have not left the Government with no recourse in a genuine emergency.
It is ironic that the Conservative Government should be taking this action because it has made somewhat of a parliamentary career for 30 years of condemning the Liberals for unilateral action with such things as closure. It is ironic that it is a Conservative Government that is attempting this final victory for unilateral action.
We have seen unilateral action in the past, such as when the Liberals revised the Standing Orders in 1969. But we thought we had surpassed such action in the early 1980s, and reached a new era of parliamentary reform. As recently as last year, when the Government was considering amending certain Standing Orders unilaterally, it was prevailed upon to come to an agreement rather than break the consensus which had been reached in the early 1980s, that parliamentary reform should only occur with unanimous consent. Finally, after we bargained and negotiated, there was an agreement, and that period of true parliamentary reform was extended.
Now it has been broken by the motion to extend the sittings. We are becoming used to closure motions as part of parliamentary life. It does not bring the same outrage as it did during the pipeline debate in 1956, when closure had not been used for decades before.
The repeated use of closure is partly a problem of the Government's impatience, but is also due to the fact that we have never really grasped the nettle of legislative planning. The Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) is here and he knows that one of the matters with which the reform committee did not deal was the whole question of legislative planning. A new committee on parliamentary reform should concern itself with that issue because it is one of the problems with this place. Rather than a process whereby we can agree what will be discussed and when, we are reduced to a game of cat and mouse each day when matters are brought up for debate when critics are not available or have been given little notice.
That is hardly a responsible or intelligent way to run the business of the country or of this Parliament.
The problem of legislative planning must be addressed.
In the final analysis, I am concerned about the spirit of unilateralism by which the Government, through the use of this motion, has declared that it can basically change any Standing Order it wishes. The Speaker argued, perhaps quite properly in a technical sense, that this power exists within the standing Orders. However, I ask Hon. Members, particularly Conservative Members, to reflect on the great emphasis they
Extension of Sittings
placed on the notion of convention in the 1982 constitutional debate. While many things are technically possible, whether under the Standing Orders in Parliament or under the law outside of Parliament, are all things permissible? What we see here is the victory of Nietzsche over Parliament. If it is technically possible, do it.
It is a parliamentary equivalent to Dostoevsky's Raskolnikov in Crime and Punishment. The Government has to prove itself in the way Raskolnikov wanted to show he was above ordinary morality and killed the old woman.
In this case, a parliamentary majority wants to show that it is above the morality of opposition or minority rights in Parliament. It is parliamentary ubermenschen. That is actually what is happening.
What is incredible about it is that because of this motion and the use of the Standing Orders in that way, everything is possible and, in the eyes of the Government, everything is permissible. The Opposition is no longer seen to be operating within an agreed upon set of rules which it uses to advance what it thinks to be in the interests of the nation.
If we happen to think that retarding the progress of the free trade agreement is in the interests of Canada, we have every right to do that here in the House of Commons. That is what the House of Commons is for. The Government has every right to use agreed upon rules to advance its view that the free trade agreement is good for Canada. What it does not have the right to do is to say to the Opposition: "When you start to get the better of us, we are going to change the rules on you all by ourselves, unilaterally". Everything is permissible. That is the problem with what we have before us. The Opposition does have a right to play within the rules.
I can remember when the Liberal Government used to talk about the Conservative Opposition in the early 1980s. I came here in 1979, but in 1980, during the constitutional debate, the heat was really on. People would heap scorn on the Conservatives for using every parliamentary tactic at its disposal. Believe it or not, I used to come to its defence. I defended the Conservatives by saying that as long as they were within the rules, they are demonstrating to the Canadian people how strongly they feel about the particular measure the Government was taking and they will be judged accordingly in terms of politics. That should be the final arbiter. It should not be the Government which decides whether or not the Opposition deserves to be reprimanded for holding up the government's agenda. It should be the people who decide. It is a political judgment. If we hold up the free trade agreement or the legislation pertaining to this or that, and the people happen to agree with the Government, we are going to pay a political price. That is a choice that Oppositions have to make and it is a choice that Government's have to make.
The problem is that it is not being left to the political process. The Government will decide it. What is happening

here is that the public is having its role eroded. The Speakership is having its role eroded, because if anyone lost in this motion, it was the Speakership, when the Government said: "The powers entrusted to the Speaker by the Standing Orders to decide whether or not the parliamentary calendar will be broken will no longer reside in the Chair. They will reside in the Government".

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO EXTEND HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
The next question is on the motion of Mr. Lewis:
That, notwithstanding any Standing Order or practice of the House, from the day of adoption of this motion and until no later than Friday, September 9, 1988, the House will meet on the days and at the times specified in Standing Order 3, but not on August 1;
That, during such period, the Speaker shall adjourn the House on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays at 10.00 o'clock p.m., and on Wednesdays at 6.00 o'clock p.m., and on Fridays at 3.00 o'clock p.m., and that the provisions of Standing Order 66 relating to the adjournment proceedings shall be suspended;
That, during such period, the Standing Order respecting the daily mid-day interruption of business on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays shall not be suspended;
That, at 6.00 o'clock p.m. on Mondays, Tuesdays and Thursdays, or at the conclusion of Private Members' Business, the House shall proceed to "Government Orders" pursuant to Standing Order 22;
That this special order shall not apply on any allotted days designated in the supply period ending June 30, 1988.
The House divided on the motion, which was agreed to on the following division:
